en: The Mayūraśataka, accompanied by the two commentaries titled Bhāvabodhinī and Sūryaśatakasārthakatākhyā.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
He who delights in playing the flute, and who is the full moon to the night-lotuses of the hearts of the cowherd women.
Victorious is he who wanders in the forest of Vṛndāvana, the mass of glory belonging to Yaśodā. // 1 //

For the attainment of my desired goal, I bow to Vāgdevī, who is as white as the autumn moon and the kunda flower, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who sits in the lotus posture while bestowing both fearlessness and boons. 2.

Having remembered Vighnavināyaka with devotion for the sake of destroying the host of obstacles, and having bowed to the feet of my gurus as well, I shall undertake this work by taking refuge in them. (3)
Madhusūdana, born in the lineage of the Pañcanada [Pañjāb], the son of Mādhava Bhaṭṭa, and the disciple of the teacher Bālakṛṣṇa—the moon of the Atri clan—comments upon this *Śataka* of Ravi. (4)
For the awakening of students, a concise commentary is being composed by way of word-by-word analysis; may the learned show compassion toward it. (5)
Now, for the delight of the assembly of the learned, the account of the manifestation of the *Śrīsūryaśataka*, as known from the mouths of venerable elders, is being related. It is as follows:
[it occurred] during the reign of the King of Mālava, whose capital was Ujjayinī.
The two courtiers of the great king Śrī Harṣa, the preeminent among poets and the author of the drama titled *Ratnāvalī*.
The two great poets of the East were Bāṇa and Mayūra.
Between them, Mayūra-bhaṭṭa was the father-in-law of Bāṇa-bhaṭṭa,
the author of the *Kādambarī*.
He had a son-in-law, and between the two of them there was a mutual rivalry regarding their poetic skill.
Bāṇa, however, had previously arrived once at the presence of the king.
He was established in the king's presence with great honor;
he resided in Ujjayinī together with his family. After some days had passed,
Having heard his verses in the course of a discussion on poetry,
Mayūrabhaṭṭa was summoned by the king from his own country, accompanied by a multitude of disciples.
Accompanied by a retinue of horses, chariots, camels, swings, servants,
and other attendants, he arrived in Ujjayinī; having heard of this, the king received him with great honor in a magnificent palace.

A residence was provided near the palace of Bāṇabhaṭṭa, and provisions for his meals were sent. There, Mayūrabhaṭṭa performed his ablutions and worship of the deity, and surrounded by his disciples, he ate and remained there in contentment. Then, in the evening—
After performing his twilight devotions,
weary from the journey,
he went to an unenclosed area on the upper floor of the palace to dispel the summer heat.
He slept in a place where there was a flow of air; his disciples also attended upon him with services such as massaging his feet, fanning him, and offering betel.
Having done so, he went elsewhere at his command and fell asleep. Then Mayūrabhaṭṭa, rising during the Brāhma-muhūrta, performed the purification of his body,
put on two clean garments, and sat upon a seat for the purpose of meditating on the Supreme Self.
He was seated facing the east. Immediately thereafter, Bāṇabhaṭṭa’s wife— the daughter of Mayūrabhaṭṭa— rose from her husband’s bed and,
descending by way of the stairs from the upper part of the palace, was [seen] by Mayūrabhaṭṭa.
She was seen; and having seen her, mistaking her for another woman, she was described with many verses of similar form. Among them, one verse is as follows:
"Who is this woman, who has just finished her meal, whose girdle is disarrayed, and whose garment clings to her limbs with perspiration?"
At dawn, the young woman departs like a startled deer, apprehensive on all sides:
"By whom has this lotus-face, with its honey-sweet nectar, been bitten? By whom has it been drunk?
By whom has heaven been enjoyed today? Whom has the God of Love pleased, he who was struck down by the eye of Śiva? (1)

Immediately thereafter, she descended by the stairs and entered the house; however, in the body of Mayūrabhaṭṭa, who was exceedingly learned in the Vedas, [there arose] even from a sin committed through negligence.
Like a drop of ink upon a spotless garment, leprosy suddenly appeared on him. Seeing this deformity upon his own body, he quickly descended from the palace,
covered his body with a cloth inside the house, and sat down, reflecting:
"Aha! What is this sudden transformation of my state? I do not recall having committed any sin whatsoever from birth until now, even through my knowledge; yet today, at dawn—"
"Except for describing another's wife—let it be; first, I shall reflect upon it. Having said this, he summoned his dear disciple and spoke:
"Long-lived one, you must go..."
"You must investigate thoroughly which mansion on the seventh floor near our residence belongs to whom. Having said, "So be it," he went there, investigated,
and returned, saying, "O Teacher, this is the mansion of your son-in-law, Bāṇabhaṭṭa."

Having heard that, he fell into great despondency and thought: "Alas! That daughter of mine was described by me, who am devoid of fortune; this is the fruit of that. Therefore, from now on, let me perform the praise of the glorious Sun and, having removed his leprosy,"

Having resolved, "I shall perform an expiation for my sin at the end of this body," he said to his beloved disciple: "Long-lived one, I command you to perform a certain task; it must be done by you without hesitation. When the disciple replied, "So be it," he spoke again: "Today is the day Śini."
"I must observe a fast and remain indoors. If any royal official or anyone else comes seeking an audience with me, he should be told this: 'The Guru is exhausted from the journey.'"

"Yesterday evening he ate; because his food has not yet been digested, he remains today lying down inside, afflicted by fever and a headache. And when the time arrives, you, together with the circle of disciples, [should perform] the worship of the deity."

Having prepared it, one should eat; food must be given to the circle of dependents and to the horses, oxen, and so forth. At the door of the house, someone must remain standing steadfastly so that no one may enter unnoticed within.

He approached and said: "Not even one from among the circle of disciples should come into my presence uninvited, and you must not stand too far away. Furthermore, today you must go to the bank of the Śiprā, identify a large tree in a secluded spot, and at evening twilight, [climb] onto a branch above it."
A sling made of sixty-four cords must be fastened; many loads of wood are to be brought there.

During the latter part of the night, while I am sleeping on my bed with four disciples, I am to be carried to that spot as if I were about to die. You, moreover, [should bring] the requisites for the worship of the deity.

"Having taken a washed upper garment and fire, you must go there. Then he did everything exactly as he was told. In the latter part of the night, Mayūrabhaṭṭa reached the bank of the Śiprā with his disciples and said to them: "You must take your bedding and stay at a distance."
"Whoever comes by this path must be turned back. The disciples did exactly so;

however, Priyaśiṣya was stationed nearby. Having personally performed the purification of his body, bathed, and arrived at the foot of a tree, he established and kindled a fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and adorned it.

Having cast his loads of wood into the fire and summoned his dear disciple to his side, he uncovered his own body, showed it to him, and said: "Alas! Suddenly leprosy has appeared on my body; for its removal..."

"The illustrious Sūrya is being praised by me; you must remain not far away. Whatever verse I compose, take note of it and write it down on paper. Having heard this, the disciple went and stood nearby.
Then Mayūrabhaṭṭa climbed a tree and, standing in a basket facing the east at sunrise, [began to praise the Sun].
He began to praise the illustrious Sun, composing one verse at a time and cutting one rope from the scale at a time; the disciple, possessing a hundredfold retentive memory,
retained them as they were spoken and wrote them down on a leaf.

In the sequence of describing the splendor of the sun—the orb of the chariot reddened by the horses of the rays mentioned previously—one hundred and nine verses were composed. These were as suspended by cords from a carrying-pole (śikya) as they were; then, somehow grasping a single cord, he composed the hundredth verse.
At that very moment, his body became free from leprosy. Seeing this,
he rejoiced, thinking, "This has been accomplished by the grace of the glorious Sun," and began to cut the remaining rope in order to perform the final expiation for the end of his life.

At that moment, the Lord Bhāskara, being well-pleased, approached, took him by both hands, set him down upon the ground, and said: "You have become free from sin; now, ask for another boon. Then he replied: "O Blessed One, this alone is my boon—that you be my inner controller (antaryāmī)."

"Having become manifest," [the Lord said]. Furthermore, the Blessed One declared: "With a gracious mind, even though unasked, this is granted to you: living for a human lifespan, free from disease from birth until death, having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, at the end of the body you shall attain union with me (matsāyujya). And whoever [recites] these one hundred verses..."
He shall praise me, being liberated from all sins;
he shall obtain health, excellent poetic skill, intelligence, superior strength, beauty, longevity,
the most excellent knowledge, sovereignty, wealth, and happiness.
Having said, "By my grace he shall obtain [it]," the Blessed One ascended the path of the sky even as he was looking on; Mayūrabhaṭṭa also [thought], "This is a great [thing]..."

Regarding the term "prasāda": having performed one hundred prostrations with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*), he composed a verse of praise for the fruit [of the practice] in accordance with the boon granted by the illustrious Sūrya. Thereafter, having performed the midday rites and the worship of the deity, he [extinguished] the consecrated fire.

Having worshipped, bowed, and dismissed [the deity], he returned joyfully to his own residence with his disciples. Having invited other Brahmins as well and fed them, he ate together with his disciples. He spent that night in great joy with this news. This is the news.

This work was brought to light in the world by his disciples following the approval of Mayūrabhaṭṭa, who was delighted by the grace of the illustrious Sūrya. Then, at an auspicious hour in the morning, Mayūrabhaṭṭa was summoned with great honor by King Śrī Harṣa, after the king had dispatched his domestic priest and learned scholars.
Accompanied by his own disciples, he went into the presence of the king and bestowed blessings upon the king with the *Śrīsūryaśataka*. The king, being exceedingly pleased,
honored him by bestowing elephants, horses, chariots, villages, garments, ornaments, swings, palaces, and other gifts.

He was established in his own presence; having brought his family from his native land, he resided in the royal palace like Bāṇabhaṭṭa. Day after day, he gratified Śrī Harṣa with his poetic compositions.
Thus, the *Śrīsūryaśataka* appeared, consisting of one hundred verses followed by a single verse of praise for the fruit [of the work]. 0.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa! He who is the lord of all aesthetic delights, the emission of all auspicious things, the refuge of all sages, and the weapon against the darkness of the fickle-minded.
May the seven-horsed Sun be served—he who fulfills all the rites of sacrifice and charity for people, and who illumines the entire universe. 1.
Having bowed to his guru, Vaidyanātha, renowned as Pāyaguṇḍe, explains this "Hundred Verses on the Glorious Sun" composed by Mayūra for the pacification of disease. //2//
In this regard, I shall now distill the essence of the aesthetic delight found in the context of the *Śrīraviśataka*, which was respectfully imbibed from the lotus-like mouths of ancient authors.
[It concerns] the sovereign of the Mālava country, whose capital was Avantikā, and who adorned the assembly of poets.

Of the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Harṣavardhana— who is the crest-jewel of poets, a wish-fulfilling tree for supplicants, and renowned for his refined elegance in the composition of the *Ratnāvalī*, a drama by the poet Dhāvaka.
There were two ancient poets from the East, Bāṇa and Mayūra, who were jewels upon the crowns of the assembly of poets;
for instance:
In that place, Mayūrabhaṭṭa was the father-in-law, and his son-in-law was Bāṇabhaṭṭa, who was adorned by the grace of Kādambarī; between the two of them,
there was an intense mutual rivalry regarding their poetic compositions.
In that regard, having already learned of the events and being world-renowned,
he was summoned repeatedly with great respect by the king; eventually, arriving at that capital city, he stood before the king.
Having arrived with great honor and exceeding respect from the king, he was established by him in his own residence near his palace together with his retinue.
Having stayed there, he spent several days; then, while engaged in poetic composition,
the king, having respectfully drunk in the verses of the peacock, summoned him with great longing as before.
Mayūrabhaṭṭa, renowned for his righteousness, long-established, and one who has known all that is to be known, was adorned by a multitude of disciples.
Accompanied by a retinue of horses, chariots, camels, palanquins, wealth, and other attendants, he arrived at Avantikā.
Then,
having heard of his arrival, Avantikā went out to meet him, preceded by the son of the minister, the family priest, and others.

He met him with great honor and respect in the most beautiful upper chamber of Bāṇabhaṭṭa’s mansion, and having quickly gratified him by filling it with fragrant food, clothing, and various other requisites, he then—
There, Mayūrabhaṭṭa, having performed his daily duties such as bathing, twilight prayers, and the worship of deities at the appropriate time,
and having eaten according to his pleasure surrounded by his disciples,
sat upon a comfortable seat for some time, describing with great delight the ancient history related to the king.
Having settled there, and then observing the solar disc resting upon the crown of the western mountain (Asta), he performed his final duties of the evening twilight according to the prescribed rites,
and entered the interior of his palace to dispel the fatigue of the journey.

To dispel the heat of summer, he sat down comfortably and fell asleep upon a beautiful, soft bed in a pleasant location— unobstructed, whitewashed, purified by moonbeams, and filled with breezes— and his disciples did likewise.
Having performed services such as massaging his feet, fanning him, and offering water and betel-leaf,
he went elsewhere at his command and fell asleep. Then Mayūrabhaṭṭa arose during the Brahma-muhūrta, meditated upon his chosen deity, prayed to the earth, and performed the purification of his body.

Having put on two clean, washed garments, he sat upon a comfortable seat facing the east for the contemplation of the Supreme Self; with *darbha* grass and *pavitra* blades in hand, having sipped water according to ritual custom (*ācamana*) and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he took his seat.
Then, Bāṇabhaṭṭa’s wife—the daughter of Mayūrabhaṭṭa—rose from her husband’s bed.

Descending slowly by the stairway from the elevated ground of the temple, she was observed by Mayūrabhaṭṭa; and having seen her, impelled by fate and mistaking her for another woman because she possessed such a form, he described her in eight verses as follows:

Who is this young woman who, having finished her meal, goes out at dawn with her garments disheveled and her clothes clinging to her limbs with sweat, startled like a doe and suspicious of everything?
By whom has this lotus-face, with its honey-sweet nectar, been bitten, and by whom has it been drunk?
By whom has heaven been enjoyed today? By whom has the God of Love been destroyed, struck by the eye of Hara? And by whom has [Śiva] been propitiated? (1)
With her left hand she was binding her mass of hair from which sparse flowers had fallen, and with her right hand her upper garment that had slipped off; her girdle was loosened by its cord,
and with a smiling face, her hair disheveled, she held betel in her left hand, full of passion.
She, who had been brought to the bedchamber while under the sway of passion, was entreated by the one who dispels pride. //2//
Who is this woman, whose face is like the full moon, who is fair-complexioned and gazes like a deer;
whose gait is like that of a playful lordly elephant in rut or a swan, and who has made the surface of the earth beautiful with her presence;
whose mouth is cooled by fragrant breath, and who speaks words as soft as nectar?
A young man lives with his own thorn within him, he for whom such a beloved woman exists. 3.
Who is this woman with such lovely hips, intoxicated by the excess of passion?
Her curved knitting of the brows rivals the splendor of Indra’s rainbow,
and her face— a full moon and a blossoming lotus— belongs to this beautiful woman with a slender waist.
The *veṇī* is characterized by the graceful use of case-endings; the *indravajrā* is characterized by the form of a serpent. 4.
Who is this woman, possessing a face like the shimmering moon,
her limbs the color of campaka flowers, her body full and adorned with speech;
and who moves with the bold, playful, and spontaneous grace of a lioness?
Moreover, she has a face like a lotus in the sky and bestows her own bliss upon those who desire it. //5//
Who is this woman with limbs so delicate, her eyes darting as she walks with the grace of a swan;
she whose two hands—anointed with saffron and adorned with gold—are making the anklets ring?
Thus she proceeds along the path, her flowers scattered and her braid trailing as she stumbles.
Holding betel in her left hand, with a smiling face, she entered the secret chamber.
Who is this woman of fresh youth with a moon-like face walking along the lovely path—
her eyes rolling and agitated by sleep, her bimba-fruit lips ripe,
her hair disheveled, and her body marked by nail-scratches and teeth-bites?
By which Rākṣasa has this Śārdūlavikrīḍita Rati been enjoyed? // 7 //
Who is this woman, heavy with the burden of full breasts, her waist marked by yellow pigment, wandering like a doe separated from her herd, as restless and fickle as a startled gazelle;
she moves with a playful grace, yet with the slow gait of a weary, rutting lord of elephants?
Indeed, upon seeing this form that leads to the state of bodilessness, even an old man becomes filled with desire. // 8 //

Then she decorated the interior of the house; subsequently, while the foot of Mayūrabhaṭṭa— an exceedingly learned and highly virtuous man— was resting upon a clean cloth washed by negligence, it happened.
Suddenly, a leprosy appeared like a drop of ink; then, having observed this deformity in his own body, he [reflected].

Quickly descending from his lofty palace, covering himself with a garment, and entering the interior of his house, he sat down and reflected: "Aha! What is this sudden transformation that has occurred in my body?
Surely no sin whatsoever has been committed by me through knowledge or desire since birth."
"I remember. Let it be for now; rather, let me reflect upon it further, except for the description of another's wife.
Then, having summoned his dear disciple, he said: "O long-lived one, go and [investigate] thoroughly..."
Having reflected thus, one should come here, near our residence,
to the seventh floor,
which is whitened with lime and reaches toward the clouds.

"Whose palace is this? Having replied, "So be it," he went there, examined it, returned, performed a salutation, and said, "O Teacher, this is the palace of your son-in-law, Bāṇabhaṭṭa. Then, having heard that, immediately—
Having fallen into great distress, he reflected: "Alas! My daughter was described by me, who am devoid of fortune;
this is the fruit of that. From now on, let it be so: having performed the praise of the glorious Sun, I shall eliminate this leprosy at the end of his life."
"I shall perform an expiation. Having thus resolved, he then said to his beloved disciple:
"O long-lived one, a certain task is commanded by me; that you must carry out without hesitation or doubt."
"It must be welcomed," he said. When the other replied, "So be it," he spoke again:
"Today is Saturday; I must observe a fast, and that too internally."
You must remain here. Should any royal official or anyone else come seeking to see me, you should speak to him thus: "The Guru, exhausted from the journey, ate last night;
due to the indigestion of that meal, he is currently suffering internally from fever and a headache today."
"He remains after having slept," and by you as well.

Having performed the worship of the deity, the offering of food (naivedya), the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and other rites together with the circle of his disciples, he should eat at the appropriate time along with the group of servants.
And food should be caused to be given at the door of the temple for the horses, bulls, and other animals.

By what means should one remain steadfast? In such a way that no one remains unknown within, nor does anyone else enter; even among the disciples, no one should come into my presence unless summoned by someone. By you—

And you should always remain at a distance that is not too great, as is appropriate. Furthermore, today you must go to the bank of the Śiprā, and having identified a large tree in a secluded spot, [you must wait] above it in the evening darkness.
A swing-basket capable of bearing a load, made of one hundred ropes, should be fastened to the branch; many loads of wood are to be brought there. Then, during the latter part of the night—
"Accompanied by four disciples, I must be led to that place while sleeping on my bed as if I were about to die;
you too must take the implements for the worship of the deity and the fire in clean garments."
"And having gathered them, you must go there. Then he performed everything exactly as he had been told.
Subsequently, when Mayūrabhaṭṭa had been brought by them to the bank of the Śiprā during the latter part of the night, he [addressed] them...
He said to his disciples:
"You must bring a bed, go a distance away, and remain there; whoever comes along this path is to be turned back."
The disciples did exactly so; however, his beloved disciple was stationed nearby.

Having personally performed the purification of the body, bathed, and completed the appropriate rites such as sipping water (ācamana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma), he approached the foot of a tree, established the sacred fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and—
Having adorned the funeral pyre with loads of wood and cast it into the fire, and having established a hot wind,
he summoned his beloved disciple to his side and covered his own body [with his cloak].
Having shown it, he said:
"Alas! Suddenly a leprosy has appeared on my body; therefore, for its removal, the glorious Seven-Horsed One (the Sun) is being praised by me."
"You must remain not very far away while I recite the verse."

"Having ascertained that, it should be written on the document. Having heard this, he stood nearby together with his disciples. Then Mayūrabhaṭṭa, having climbed a tree, stood facing the front of the scale-bowl.
At dawn,
having composed a single verse each to praise the glorious Sun, the disciple Śatādhvī cut one rope of the scale at a time.
Having determined each of those [names], he wrote them down upon a leaf; thus,
in the sequence of the previously mentioned solar orb— the chariot-circle of the dawn-red horses of the rays— he recorded ninety-nine [names].
The verses were cut away one by one; that many cords of the swing were also severed.
Then, somehow managing to hold onto a single cord, he composed the hundredth verse, and at that very moment, his body became free of leprosy.
Having observed that, [he thought], "This has been accomplished through the grace of the illustrious Sūrya," and having attained joy, he performed the expiation for the end of his body.
He began to cut the remaining rope; immediately, the Blessed Lord Bhāskara, being well-pleased,
approached him.
Having lifted him up, set him down upon the ground, and touched his body with his hand while embracing him, he said, "You have become free from sin."
"Now ask for another boon," [the Lord said]. Then he replied, "O Blessed One, this alone is my boon: that you, the Inner Controller, have become manifest before me."
Then the Blessed One said: "Out of faith, I shall grant this even though it was not requested.
Living out the full span of a human life, free from disease throughout his lifetime, he shall enjoy all worldly pleasures."
At the end of the body, you shall attain union with me; and whoever praises me with these one hundred verses shall be freed from all sins and obtain health and true poetic skill.
"By my grace, he shall obtain intelligence, superior strength, beauty, long life, learning, sovereignty, wealth, and happiness.
Having spoken thus, while he was looking on, the Blessed One [emitted] a garland of rays.

Having ascended to the path of the sky, Mayūrabhaṭṭa, thinking "this is a great favor," performed one hundred and eight prostrations with his limbs touching the ground, in accordance with the boon granted by the illustrious Sūrya.
He composed a single verse in praise of the fruit [of his merit]. Then, having performed the midday rites and the worship of the deity, he fully honored the consecrated fire,
circumambulated it, and prostrated before it with the eight limbs touching the ground (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
Having performed the expiation for the violation of his vow regarding the end of his life,
and having dismissed [the officiants], he returned to his own residence surrounded by his disciples; then, being filled with joy,
he invited the Brahmins, honored them, fed them, and [remained] together with his family.
He enjoyed [the feast] and passed that night with great joy in this conversation;
then, with the consent of Mayūrabhaṭṭa, who was delighted by the favor of the illustrious Sūrya, he—
The matter was brought before the disciples by the world;
then,
at an auspicious moment, having dispatched the family priest and learned men with great reverence.
Summoned by King Śrī Harṣa, Mayūrabhaṭṭa, having performed his morning rites, arrived at the royal palace with his disciples;
the king went to the palace gate, received him, and escorted him into the assembly hall.
Having been honored and seated upon a most beautiful and lofty throne, he prostrated himself, and having sat down in his proper place,
he bestowed blessings upon the king with the *Śrīsūryaśataka*.
When the king’s two sons were thus highly praised by all those members of the assembly, poets, and scholars, the king was exceedingly pleased.
Having entreated him, saying, "Please honor me by accepting elephants, horses, chariots, villages, dwellings, ornaments, swings, palaces, wealth,
and so forth, and remain right here in my presence," [he requested him] to go to his palace.
Having been granted permission with the traditional formalities of rising from one's seat,
he entered his own residence;
then, by the king's command, having brought his family from his native land, [he settled] in the palace provided by the king.

Like Bāṇabhaṭṭa, he constantly delighted King Śrī Harṣa with his own ever-new lotuses of verses. Thus, the *Śrīsūryaśataka* appeared, consisting of one hundred verses plus a single verse of praise for the fruit [of the work]. The meter of this century of verses is known as Sragdharā.

This is proclaimed as *Sragdharā*, characterized by three *mra*, *bha*, *na*, and *ya* gaṇas in each quarter, joined with the pause of the three sages (the *yati* at the 7th and 14th syllables), according to its definition stated in the *Vṛttaratnākara*.
Therein, the description of the rays is in forty-three verses; thereafter, the description of the horse is in six verses;
thereafter, the description of Aruṇa is in eleven verses; and thereafter, in twelve [verses].
The description of the chariot; then, the description of the maṇḍala with eight verses;

then, the description of the Blessed Lord with twenty verses; and finally, one verse in praise of the fruit—this is the discernment to be understood. Furthermore, the ultimate purport of all these verses is as follows:
The primary purport is precisely that which was stated previously: the cessation of the undesirable and so forth. However, the intermediate purports will become clear in their respective places.
In this regard, [this work] is commenced by me for the sake of pacifying fear and evil for myself.
Since leprosy and obstacles are of the nature of powerful sins,

this [work] is characterized by an auspicious invocation consisting of the mention of the object known as Indra— who is renowned for being the vanquisher of the Daitya Jambha, who was even more powerful than they— and which must necessarily be praised.
The author of the work performs an auspicious invocation consisting of the blessing of the Sun-god:
"To him who bears the thick dust of vermilion like the blood flowing from the frontal globes of the elephants of the enemy of Jambha..."
Like the one born from a jar (Agastya),
they are as if drenched by streams of liquid mineral-ores from the slopes of the mountain of sunrise, flowing toward that jar-born sage.
May the two red ones—
the rising sun and the dawn— come together at the same time as the splendor of the lotus grove, for our prosperity.
May the ever-new rays of the sun, illuminating the world, become equal in duration to the one who is coming. 1.
The radiant rays, belonging to the sun, may they be for your prosperity. Of what nature are these rays? They are ever-new, fresh.
Arising at dawn, what are they like? Illuminating—that is, making manifest—the world, the universe.
Again, what are they like? Reddish, or rosy; here, a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) is suggested: like what? Like the *jambha* [fruit].
[The mountain] which, as if bearing that thick vermilion dust arising from the frontal globes of Airāvata— the elephant of Indra, the slayer of Jambha— first [appeared] in the east...

Because they have risen in that direction; the meaning is that they appear reddish due to contact with the vermilion from the frontal globes of elephants stationed there. Furthermore, what are they like? "Udaya..."—the minerals such as white chalk and red arsenic belonging to the slopes of the mountain of sunrise (Udayagiri).

They are as if sprinkled by the torrents—the streams of the liquid essence of that flow which has spread here and there through its connection with the cascades. Furthermore, how are they? "As if coming," meaning simultaneously.

They are reddened by the luster—the radiance—of the lotus groves as they arrive simultaneously; here, in the final word, there is the alliteration (anuprāsa) of the letter *bha*. According to Amarasimha, "bhānu" denotes both a ray and the sun.

These [verses] belong to Bhānu; the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*, and for that, the substitution of *īya* is made by the rule *ayanādibhyaḥ*. The meter of this century of verses (*padyaśataka*) is called *sragdharā*. Its definition, however, is found in the *Vṛttaratnākara*:
This is proclaimed as Sragdharā, consisting of three feet with eleven syllables each, endowed with the meter of the three sages (the Vedic *trimuni*). Thus [ends the section]. 1.
He says, "Jambheti. The Bhānavīyas are those related to the sun; may the rays (bhānavaḥ) of the sun be for your prosperity (vibhūtyai), that is, for your sovereignty (aiśvaryāya).

Of what nature are they? They are rays (*bhānavaḥ*) that are fresh (*abhinavāḥ*), new (*navīnāḥ*), arising at the time of dawn; therefore, they illuminate (*bhāsayantaḥ*) the world (*bhuvanam*), that is, the earthly realm (*bhūloka*), by dispelling darkness.
For this very reason...
"Red" means crimson; here it is imagined in three ways.
Like what? Like [the blood] of Jambha, a specific type of demon (daitya), who was his enemy.

[The city] which bears that thick, dense powder of vermilion (sindūra) arising from the frontal globes (kumbha) of the elephant Airāvata— the mount of Indra, the enemy (ibha)— who is the adversary (arāti) of Jambha; or [it is the city] where such a thick, dense powder of vermilion arises from the frontal globes of the elephant of the eastern quarter.
Sindūra is applied for the sake of beauty;
of what kind is it?
First, by its rising in the eastern direction, it is situated upon the frontal globes of the elephant Airāvata.

The meaning is that they are "Vāruṇas" due to contact with vermilion (*sindūra*). The slopes (*taṭī*) are the peripheral regions of the mountain of sunrise; their minerals (*dhātavaḥ*) are the white chalk (*gaurika*) and red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*).
The "liquid" (*dravaḥ*) refers to the essence of the stream (*dhārā*)—that is, the row—of those minerals, which, through its connection to a waterfall (*nirjhara*), flows here and there.
As if sprinkled by the spreading floods and currents of that [river],
equal to the suns in significance,
simultaneously— as it were— at the very moment when the forest of *kāmalās* (jaundice/desires) was approaching.
By its luster and beauty, it is reddish, slightly crimson, as if colored;
this is indicated here by three words.
In the solar orb, there is a natural vermilion-redness;
it is the flow of liquid mineral streams from wearing vermilion powder,
possessing the splendor of a lotus grove, and reddened by the rays of the moon.
Because it is imagined as a cause,
there may also be three types of *utprekṣā*— namely, those consisting of a thing (*vastu*), a cause (*hetu*), and a fruit (*phala*)— according to its definition. Here,
the emotion directed toward the sun resides within the poet.

Because of that very excellence, the nature of *dhvani* in poetry is described as "the absence of [mere] devotion toward objects such as gods"; for its definition is stated by the learned: "When the suggested meaning is superior to the expressed, it is called *dhvani*. This applies similarly hereafter. In the final quarter of this verse, there is an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) of the letter *bha*: *bhānū*.
"Raśmidivākarau" is according to Amarasimha. "Bhūyāsuḥ" is the optative suffix (liṅ) used in the sense of a benediction. 1.
The hollow interior of the lotus-bud hut, for the sake of giving to those who are bowed down by devotion,
[is] the hollow interior of the lotus-bud hut; the lotus-bud.
As if desiring to attract Lakṣmī, as if opening the lotus groves; so it was seen.
May he who is skilled in destroying the terror of the world fallen into the darkness of the forms of time— may he protect us. May he protect us.
May those rays of the sun, possessing the luster of young shoots, bring you auspiciousness in all your actions. //2//
It is auspicious;
it is the auspiciousness of the sun.
May those rays of yours bring auspiciousness in your actions. Of what nature are they?

They possess the luster of young sprouts, being slightly reddish due to their tenderness from having just arisen. It is a fitting convention that the hands of others who possess excellent marks are also reddish; [for they perform] drawing forth, attracting, giving, and protecting those who are afraid.
And it is also their very function to do so. Who are they? They are those who perform the opening of the stainless forest;

this is what is being poetically imagined here. Like what? As if desirous of attracting and bestowing *lakṣmī* (fortune) upon people who are bowed down by devotion, who are humble with devotion. What kind of *lakṣmī*? The one called *kamalā* (the lotus).

She who was hidden within the interior— the hollow of that which is like a cave— namely the center of the lotus's bud, which is the dwelling-place of Śiva; she who remained concealed within the house, Lakṣmī.
The meaning is that they desire to draw [the world] forth by force and give it to their devotee. Furthermore, of what nature are they?

"Kāla" means that their form is black (kālākāra), and moreover, they are like Kāla, the Destroyer (kṛtānta), because they illuminate the universe. Such is the darkness that has fallen upon their faces; they are capable of destroying the terror of the world.

"Ready" (*sajjāḥ*) means "equipped with their own implements. "Opening" (*udghāṭanam*) is the form derived from the root *ghaṭ* belonging to the *curādika* class, used here in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). According to Amara, "kalya," "sajja," and "nirāmaya" are synonyms;
likewise, "bali," "hasta," "aṃśu," and "kara" are synonyms for tax.

Regarding the words *kāla* (time) and *kalpa* (aeon), the reading with the dental *u* as the penultimate letter (*auṣṭhya-upadha*)—namely *kālau* and *kalpāḥ*—is not authoritative, because it would result in the disruption of the alliteration of the consonant *l*. //2//
The rays— meaning the beams— of you, Bhāskara, are thus to be described; may they likewise bring about your welfare hereafter, as before.
Let them act. Of what nature are they? Their splendor is like that of a *kisalaya*, a fresh sprout;
thus, due to their freshness and tenderness, they are slightly reddened. It is a matter of propriety that the hands of others who possess auspicious marks are also reddish.
Unveiling, attracting,
bestowing, and protecting those who are afraid are likewise indeed the functions of the hand.
It is worldly. Who are they? They are those who cause the multitude of lotuses to bloom; here, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is expressed:
[the sun] desires the longing to attract or seize *lakṣmī*—meaning beauty or prosperity—in order to give it to his own servant, who is bowed down by devotion, humble with devotion.

For whom [the rays] are as if such; and this is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result), because the expansion of the lotus grove— which is established by the very nature of the sun’s rays—
is first apprehended and then [imagined] as the result of the gift of Lakṣmī, which is the primary fruit of the praise.

Because of conceptualization; as for its characteristic, it has been explained previously. Of what nature is it? It is hidden, well-concealed, within the interior—the inner space—of that which is like a *niṭakuṭa*, namely the hollow, the middle, of that very cottage, a specific type of dwelling, which is the bud or center of a lotus. Or else: [it is] hidden there.
The bud of a lotus is its *puṭa*; that bud is like a *saṃpuṭa*, a closed casket, hence "that lotus-casket. That itself is a hut (*kuṭī*), as before;
its hollow interior (*koṭara*) is [the place] within it.
In her lap— that is, in the hollow within its center, which is like a bosom— she was either hidden or clinging there; having remained concealed within, she was Lakṣmī, O Blessed One,
the impeller of wealth.

The meaning is that they, being connoisseurs of the quality of granting all desired objects, wish to bestow them upon the supplicant devotee, having drawn [the goddess] forth from the lotus. And since her dwelling is the lotus forest, its blossoming occurs; for even another person [might do so], having hidden her within the house.
It is well known that [the deity] opens [the vessel], seizes it by force, and gives it away.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? He has the form (*ākāra*) of *kāla*, meaning his color is black (*kṛṣṇavarṇa*), and moreover, his form or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is like that of *Kāla*, the Ender (*kṛtānta*).
Because it swallows the world, such darkness has a face; its "utkṛṣṭapradeśa" (exalted region) is like that face.

By chance, the world fell there, and those who are capable—meaning skilled—in the destruction or annihilation of the terror and fear of that world, [are described as follows]. This refers to the sense of "opening," derived from the root *ghaṭ* in the meaning of "assembling."

The form [of the word] occurs in the sense of being a friend to thieves and others in the *tyuṭ* suffix; "hands, rays, and taxes" are synonyms for *kara*, according to Amara; and "the end-maker, laughter, and time" are synonyms for *kāla*; in reality, they are [synonyms for] destruction and dissolution (*dhvaṃsa-kalpa*).

This is the reading; however, it is not in verse because it would result in the disruption of the alliteration (*anuprāsa*), for which the meaning is "careful" (*sāvadhānā*). According to Amarasimha, "kalyau" means "healthy" (*sajjānī-ārāmayau*).
In this case, the details regarding the limbs and so forth are as previously stated. //2//

Falling alike upon the interiors of lotuses and upon the sharp peaks of mountains— [the raindrops] falling upon the interiors of the waters... [the raindrops] falling upon the interiors of the waters.
May those [rays] which are uniform at the beginning and at the conclusion of the day,
proceeding without alternation in the courtyard of the abode of the three worlds, protect you.
The rays of the sun, intensely bearing heat produced by their continuous journey through the sky like one who has set out on a long road, have begun to fall.
May the rays— the feet— of Bradhna, the Sun, protect you, as if born of labor. Of what kind are they?
"In the calyxes" means: falling simultaneously at the same time into the calyxes—the inner paths—of lotuses, and upon the sharp-peaked *śikhara* trees and mountains.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? "At the commencement," meaning at the very beginning of the day, in that same manner.
At the moment of their cessation and at the time of their completion, they are uniform in form, being tender and reddish.

Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Without succession" (*niṣparyāyam*); that is, the three worlds themselves are the *bhavana* (abode), and its courtyard is the central portion—within that, there is no succession.
They proceed simultaneously, whereas the feet of others proceed only in succession;
this is the meaning of their being distinct. Furthermore, of what nature are they? Excessively hot.
What are they like? They are as if born from the continuous fatigue of a long journey—that is, produced by the exhaustion of a path that can be traversed without interruption.
Their natural heat is poetically imagined (utprekṣate) as being born from the toil of such a journey. According to Amara, *taru* means tree and *śaila* means mountain or peak (*śikhariṇ*).
The terms *pāda*, *raśmi*, *aṅghri*, and *turyāṃśa* are also used [to denote a fourth part]. //3//
May the rays of the sun— the feet of the radiant one— protect and guard you.
According to Amara, "pāda" refers to a ray and a quarter.

Of what nature are they? They are intensely, utterly hot, bearing—that is, possessing—heat. Here, it is poetically imagined that this is the fatigue from the journey caused by their continuous movement.
It is as if the exhaustion produced by the fatigue of walking along the road;
and since its nature is uniform, even the activities [of the mind] are suitable as effects of the feet,
as well as other causes of exhaustion.
In order to indicate [this] by means of the other foot,
and to demonstrate its similarity through the indication of a slight difference,
he states three qualifiers: "that world which has three parts."
The entire universe is that very abode or home; as if in its courtyard—in the middle space of the courtyard—they proceeded in a manner that was nonsensical and devoid of sequence. Therein...
Simultaneously and at once, upon the interiors— the central regions— of the lotuses (*ambhoruha*), and upon the mountain peaks (*śikhara*) characterized by sharp points and keen summits.
"Simultaneously" (*akramaṃ*) means: those which, while falling and spreading forth, fall in exactly the same manner at every point;

those which are of one form (*ekarūpāḥ*), having a single nature, being identical at the beginning of the day—the time of sunrise—and at the time of cessation—the time of twilight; these are the "feet" (*pādāḥ*) as they are well-known in the world.
They protect [the world] in succession; thus, the feet of the Blessed One are the most excellent even in their very nature as feet. For this very reason, the term "foot" (pāda) is used as a synonym;
otherwise, one would have spoken of "feet" (caraṇa) and so forth. Here, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction/superiority) is intended. //3//
When the darkness has fallen away from the luster of their upper garments, they first behold those whose veils have been removed; then the upper garment falls away.
The upper garment falls away. The upper garment falls away.
Just as the sun of fierce rays spreads forth its beams, so does he spread forth his creatures like threads;
he spreads them out with a slender body,
and with a slender body he bestows wealth.
Having instantly become dense, they [the rays] of yours have become vast, pervading the ten directions which are gradually becoming clear.
Me.
Constantly producing a stainless sky, may they grant you abundant auspiciousness. // 4 //
May those rays of yours bestow—that is, grant—excellent and abundant auspiciousness. Which ones? Those rays which the hot-rayed sun, the Sun, previously emitted.
He spreads out—that is, he extends—many things in this very manner. Like what? Like threads, as if they were threads.

Having done what? Having seen living beings (*jantu*) freed from their veils—that is, rendered unobstructed. Under what condition? When there is the luster of an upper garment—that is, when there is the darkness of an upper garment.

The meaning is that when [the world] was falling away, he beheld sentient beings without protection and, out of compassion, extended those which are in the form of threads for their protection. What are they like? Immediately becoming dense...

They are producing a stainless garment, that is, the sky; in the sense of rays of light, "stainless" is an attributive adjective of the predicate, meaning they are making the sky, the atmosphere, pure. In the sense of threads, it means they are producing a bright, clear garment, that is, cloth.
What kind of garment? "Krama" means that which clearly pervades the ten states,
that is, the ten directions.

In this way, it is "vast" because of the rows (*ālya*)—that is, lines—of ten fringes (*daśā*) arranged both crosswise and lengthwise upon the edges of ten cloths; for fringes also exist on the edge of any other cloth.
Although, according to the statement in the first half [of the verse], it should have been said "those which consist of threads,"...

The sun of fierce rays spreads forth its beams, and by them they produce the sky; nevertheless, because the quality [of producing] is easily accomplished, the latter half of the verse describes the object itself as the agent, as if it were the agent of the action. Regarding the word *marīci*, Amara states: "The word *marīci* is used for both feminine and neuter."
The word *ambara* means the sky, as well as garments. // 4 //

Having become dense— that is, having attained an unreal compactness— gradually, year by year, they cause the ten directions (daśa āśāḥ), which are clear and transparent, to become vast and pure, stainless space (ambaram ākāśam), by means of those very ten directions themselves, which constitute a row of ten (daśālī).

May those rays, as they act, bestow—that is, grant—auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) to you; which rays? Those rays which the hot-rayed sun (*tigmarociḥ sūryaḥ*) spreads out extensively (*atanu*) in the east (*prāk*) so that they may become vast.
Having done what? Having beheld—having seen—the creatures, the living beings, whose veils had been removed as the darkness, which possessed the luster of an upper garment, was falling away;
and here he provides an illustration: "just as a weaver [sees] the threads [of the world]."
Seeing them naked when their upper garments have fallen away, she first spreads out threads and fibers;
these too become clear, gradually manifesting in the form of the ten directions.
The meaning is that she produces a vast garment (*ambara*) by means of a fringe (*daśālī*) consisting of ten rows (*daśaśreṇi*). Here, the simile is explicit. //4//

As if out of grief for the moon, the lord of herbs, whose luster has been stolen away, [the sun] eclipses the herbs that have lost their light; as if out of grief for the moon, [the sun] eclipses the herbs that have lost their light.
As if first greeted by the fire rising from a shining rock;
[the phrase] "bhāsvadgrāvodgatena" means "by that which has risen from a shining rock.
(Alternatively: "bhāsvadgrāvohatena")
Displaying rocks that appeared as if dripping with blood from the wounds of severed wings at dawn;
appearing as if dripping with blood.
May the rising of the rays of the intensely radiant sun, which dispels what is undesirable, be for your welfare—[rays] that are crimson-red. 5.
Copper-red;
the emergence of the rays of the copper-colored sun, which possesses intense heat.

May the rising of the rays be for you the dispeller of what is undesirable— that is, may it serve to remove misfortune— provided that the Lord of Herbs, the Moon, has had his luster stolen away, his beauty ravished; for,
out of grief precisely at the loss of their master’s splendor, the herbs have become devoid of light, as if they were women whose husbands are away from home.

"Surpassing" means eclipsing by its own brilliance; "surpassing along with that" means outshining it together with that [brilliance]. Of what sort [are they]? "Radiant," etc.; "radiant stone" refers to the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*).
Then, as if having already risen first by the fire that had flared up—
meaning that the fire had risen for its own protection out of fear upon seeing the eclipsing of the moon and other luminaries— what was it doing further? At the time of dawn.

He showed the rocks—the stones—of the mountain, the eastern peak (Udayaparvata), as if they were dripping with the blood from the wounds of the amputation of wings formerly inflicted by Indra; showing them as if they were shedding that very blood from the scars of the wound caused by that previous severing of the wings. Of what nature was he? A protector.
It is reddish; therefore, the meaning is that from seeing the rock pervaded by it, people experience the delusion that blood is flowing. //5//

May the emergence of the rays—the rising of the beams—of the fiercely radiant sun, which is slightly copper-red, be for the removal of what is not desired, that is, for the dispelling of misfortune, for you all. Furthermore, while the Lord of Herbs, the Moon, has had its luster stolen away, its brilliance shattered, as if out of grief (śucā) for this very reason; may it be so.
Having surpassed those herbs whose luster had faded while she was away, she now eclipses them with her own radiance at the foot of the eastern mountain at dawn.
When he displayed those rocks like stones that had been wounded by the severing of their wings and were now shedding blood from them, such was his form.
Then those red rays were seen;

it was further imagined that they appeared as if their emergence had been brought about by the fire arising from sun-crystals (sūryakānta) when the sun first rose, just as another person rises to welcome someone worthy of honor who is approaching.
The resonance [of the teaching] is that one practices rising up from one's seat [in respect]. //5//
With their noses, feet, and hands shattered, and with mangled limbs covered in wounds, they uttered hoarse and indistinct cries.
One [the world] again joins together those long-sniffed at by the floods of sins; the other makes them healthy.
"Long-sniffed at" means long-extended.
May the rays of that Sun, whose unimpeded movement destroys the intense heat within you with redoubled compassion,
and which have been honored with offerings by hosts of Siddhas, swiftly effect the destruction of your sins.
May the rays, the beams of heat, of that sun, the possessor of warm rays, bestow [favor] upon him; may they place [it] within him.
May he quickly bring about the destruction of your afflictions— that is, the removal of your sins— who is the one, the peerless one, who heals such men as these, making them free from disease.

"Creating" means that he again joins them together, connecting them with their noses and so forth. Of what sort are they? "Decayed," meaning those whose rows of noses and hands have been worn away by diseases such as leprosy.
Again, of what sort are they? They are characterized by "mutilated" limbs—that is, by body parts possessing wounds.

The remainder [of the description]: Furthermore, of what kind are they? Those whose speech-sound—the sound of their utterance—is a *gharghara*, an indistinct noise imitating the sound *gharghara*. Furthermore, of what kind are they? As indicated by the word "long" (*dīrgha*): those who have been long-sniffed—that is, for a long time (*dīrgham*) over a prolonged period—by the masses of sins (*aghodhaiḥ*), due to their own service [to them].
The limit of the previous time;
"scented" means swallowed by the manifestation of fruit. Of what kind of sun? "Within"—that is, within the heart.
He whose unimpeded activity is doublefold— dense, thick,
compassionate, devoted to those [who seek refuge], dependent on them, free from obstacles, and unobstructed— [is so] because his heart is softened by compassion toward his own servants.

The meaning is: "of one who is acting swiftly for the sake of dispelling that disease. Of what kind are the clouds? [They are those] by the hosts of Siddhas stationed on the Mountain of Sunrise during the morning twilight.

Regarding the reading "dattorghoye rabhyaste": the reading of the letter *gha* in "aṅghripāṇinityakṣarānuprāsabhramāt" is not from heaven (i.e., it is an error). The correct reading is "ahni pāṇīniti. [This is derived] from the root *ahi-gatau* with an *auṇādika* suffix.
Because that [result] is established by means of the agentive suffix (*kartari-pratyaya*). Furthermore, there is no absolute loss of alliteration either,
since the letter *ha* possesses qualities such as being voiced (*ghoṣavat*).

Because the letter *gha* also shares such a common characteristic [of being a voiced aspirate], for this very reason the poet employed the letter *ha* once again in the phrase *aṃhovighātam*. [The term] *ullāghayan* means making *ullāgha*, that is, making free from disease (*nīroga*). The word *ullāgha* is derived from the root *lagh* when it is not preceded by a prefix, according to the rule beginning with *phulla* and so forth.

[He] was struck down. Then, from the causative form *karoti* (with the suffix *ṇic*), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied [to form *kārayat*]. According to Amara, *ullāgha* means "freed from disease," and *adhīna* also means "dependent."
And in the verse "gabhastighṛṇipṛśnayaḥ," there is an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) of the letter *gha*. // 6 //
May the rays— meaning the beams— of that sun, whose heat is fierce, quickly effect for you the destruction of distress, that is, the eradication of sin. Of what kind [is he]?
Within, he is endowed with extreme compassion— compassion that is doubled, more intense, dense, and firm, and which is devoted to it, extensive, free from obstacles, and constant in its operation.
[This refers to] the manifestation [of light]. Of what nature are they? Those rays of his from which an *argha* offering has been given by hosts of perfected beings (*siddha*).

Each single ray, through floods of evil—the masses of sins—[reaches] those who have been long-sniffed, meaning those pervaded for an exceedingly long time and completely filled with that; and likewise, it is well known as *gharghara*.

He heals those whose noses, feet, and hands have been shattered—that is, those with collapsed noses, feet, and hands—making them free from disease by removing their ailments, and restores them once again.
Here, *dvandvaga* refers to people afflicted by pairs [of such injuries]. He unites them once more.
May the rays of the Sun, which first assumed a dwarfed state and then likewise became tall, grant you freedom from the state of being dwarfed—
that is, the state of being humble.
Having traversed the intermediate space of the sky, they then filled the ten directions; thereafter,
like powerful enemies of the gods snatching away the darkness, those mighty ones swiftly pervaded the entire universe.
May the sons of Hari, who are powerful, who perform difficult feats with ease, and who cause even Hara to laugh, protect you—those whose horses are tawny. 7.

May the rays belonging to the one with bay horses (the Sun) remove your difficult skin diseases; may they raise you up from your hardships. May the rays related to the one with bay horses take away your leprosy and ailments.

Of what sort are they? "Rays" (*aṃśavaḥ*). By means of the playful sport (*helālīlā*) of their rising and falling, they have laughed at Hari-Viṣṇu; by these adjectives, he expresses their similarity to Hari.

"Vibhrāṇāḥ" (bearing): first, in the morning, by virtue of having spread over only a small area, they bear a state of being dwarfed and short; Hari also, prior to requesting land measured by three paces, maintained a state of being a dwarf. Furthermore, of what nature are they? Now—
Immediately thereafter, likewise tall and lofty like Hari; how were they further characterized?
They were such that they had traversed the intermediate space, the interior of the sky. Hari was also like that;
subsequently, filling the ten directions with their own bodies, Hari was likewise. Even after that, and even beyond that.

Having forcibly snatched away the entire three worlds from the darkness and swiftly pervading everywhere— just as Hari, having snatched the three worlds from Bali, the king of the Daityas, swiftly pervaded them everywhere like ash.

Pervading—of what kind of *bali* (oblation) from the enemy of the gods (*devadviṣ*)? From that which is hostile to the gods, Indra and the others. Of what kind of darkness? [It is] the enemy of the gods; that is, the enemy of the senses (*indriya*), such as the eyes and so forth, because therein they are incapable of their respective functions. Thus...

Thus far, there is a similarity between these [demons] and Hari; however, the cause of their laughter is that Hari performed this once through his illusory power (*māyā*), whereas these [demons] perform it every day before everyone's very eyes. Therefore, there is a superiority on the part of these [demons].
"Deva" refers to the king Sureghana; "devam" is explained as the senses (*indriya*), according to the *Viśva* lexicon. // 7 //

May the golden-horsed ones—the rays of the Sun, whose horses are golden—remove our hardships and sins; for by them, Viṣṇu (Hari) has been mocked, laughed at, and made to appear like an ordinary person in His playful display of rising. How so?
First, they assumed the state of being dwarfish and stunted; immediately thereafter, in that very same manner, they became tall and lofty; and following that, subsequently.
Having traversed the interior of space by means of their movement,
they then proceeded even beyond that into the ten directions.

Fulfilling [all desires] according to the maxim of the central gem (madhyamaṇinyāya), they nevertheless quickly and swiftly pervade the universe by tearing asunder— that is, separating from— the darkness of gloom.
They pervaded [the world]. From what, as it were?
Like from the enemy of the gods named Bala, a particular Daitya. For Hari also, first there was dwarfhood (*vāmanatva*), then swiftness (*prāśutva*), and then...

The meaning is as follows: first, there is the state of having traversed the interior of space; then, the state of filling the ten directions with strength; then, having covered the entire universe, the state of pervading the world with a sudden "maṭhi" sound. // 7 //
May those rays of the sun grant you prosperity—rays which, through their intense redness, greatly enhance the crimson hue of Aruṇa;
which possess the luster of blood from wounds inflicted by bits upon the faces of the chariot-horses as they toss their heads;
and which bestow the status of mountain peaks upon the summits of the mountains they rest upon.
May those rays of the sun, swaying in the sky and piercing the face of the day, grant you happiness. 8.
May the rays of the hot-beamed sun grant you happiness— those rays which, through an intense and excessive redness, bestow upon Aruṇa,
the charioteer who is himself naturally red, a profuse and dense crimson hue.

Furthermore, those whose mouths— the mouths of the horses of the chariots— possess a luster like that of blood due to the wounds caused by the bits (*khalīna*), which are known in the language of the Middle Country as *kariyārī* and are tossed up by their heads; they are thus described.
Furthermore, those who bestow upon the mountains the state of being crests and the state of having their peaks adorned with garlands of red flowers—of what sort are they? "Resorted to," etc.:
they have resorted to the peaks of the mountain-trees; those by whom this is done are thus described.
The meaning is that at dawn they first spread across the mountain peaks and the tops of trees.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are "preṅkha" in the sky—that is, moving swiftly here and there.
Again, of what nature are they? They are those by whom the face of day (the dawn) has been "khacita"—that is, pervaded.
According to Amarasimha, "śikhā," "apiḍa," and "śekhara" [are synonyms for crest/top], and "taru" and "śaila" [when meaning tree and mountain] are called "śikhariṇau.
Here, there is an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) on the letter *kha*. //8//
"By the intense": may the rays of the sun (kharāṃśoḥ), that is, the sharp-rayed one, bestow—that is, grant—happiness to you (vaḥ). Which ones?
Those which, by means of an intense (udgāḍhena) and great (mahatā) ruddiness (aruṇimnā)—that is, redness (lohityena)—are reddish (aruṇāḥ), possessing a state of redness.
They perform it abundantly and excessively; and those [horses] whose mouths are shaken by the tossing of their heads—

this being the reading "dhūtāḥ," the locative case is used— those whose throats possess the luster of the blood from the wounds caused by the bits, and those who possess the state of being the crests of mountains, of the peaks.

They act as ornaments for the head; they are those who have resorted to the peaks and summits of the jagged mountains (*śikharin*). Moving or traveling through the sky (*khe*), or shining intensely, they are inlaid (*khacita*).
Those by whom the connection [is made] at the beginning of the day, and likewise that which is the path of happiness;
"sailaśiloccaya" means mountain peaks—thus says Amara. // 8 //
Bestowing joy upon all creatures with rays drawn forth and emitted at the appropriate time, scattered in every direction during the forenoon and gathering together as the day comes to rest,
these rays are like ships for crossing the ocean of worldly existence— the source of long-lasting suffering— for the Sun, the one of blazing rays.
May cows produce for you an immeasurably supreme joy among all purifying things. 9.

May the rays—the cows—of the radiant-rayed Sun produce immeasurable joy for you. Of what nature are they? They are such that, at the appropriate time, they yield milk through being drawn in, gathered, emitted, and released.

Those by whom joy is given to living beings through waters and milk; the *maricaya* clouds, having gathered water during the eight months, release those waters during the four-month rainy season (*cāturmāsya*). Cows also, having gathered milk day and night, provide it at the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). Furthermore, of what nature are they? In the forenoon...

Thus: scattered in every direction during the first part of the day, they go to their evening rest when the day ceases; that is, they undergo dissolution, gathering together and attaining a state of oneness.
The rays of light, having spread everywhere during the day, attain a state of unification at twilight for the purpose of traveling to other continents;
the cows as well go outside during the day for the purpose of grazing.
Having wandered about, they come together in the evening for the purpose of returning to the cow-pen.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Dīrgha" means they are the source (*prabhava*) of that suffering which is long-lasting and persists over a great length of time.

In that [state] where there is no existence—that is, no worldly cycle (saṃsāra)—the fear arising from it is itself dispelled; for they are like boats for crossing over that ocean, as it were. Furthermore, of what nature are they?
They are the supreme purifier among all purifiers. (The word *pāvana* retains its original gender.)
This is a statement consisting of words;
herein, the charm lies in the expression of equality through the qualifiers of both the Mārīcī rays and the cows.

Cows, too, were born from the Sun. As it is stated in the Bṛhaspati Smṛti: "Gold is the first offspring of Fire; the earth is the daughter of Brahmā; and cows are the daughters of the Sun. The genitive case in the word *pāvanānām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇe*).
"Payaḥ" means milk; "payaḥ" also means water—thus says Amara. // 9 //

"Datta" means: may the rays (gāvaḥ) of the blazing sun (dīptāśoḥ), which are the "cows," produce for you (vaḥ) immeasurable (aparimitām), that is, innumerable, joy. Of what nature are they? [They are those] appropriate for the two suitable seasons (samucitasamayayoḥ), namely, during the summer.

The compound *varṣāsvākṛṣṭāni ca tāni sṛṣṭāni ca taiḥ pūrvakālena* means "those [elements] which were drawn up during the rains and created by them at an earlier time. For this very reason, there is a correspondence according to the respective order: just as the sun indeed takes up all the vital juices (*rasa*) in the summer and releases them during the rains, so too does Manu arise from the sun, and rain arises from Manu.

From rain comes food, and from that, progeny. With such waters as milk, they bestow joy upon living beings; scattered and spread throughout every direction in each quarter during the forenoon of the day.

When the day has ended, he is possessed by fear— fear in the form of *saṃsāra*, which is the source, the place of origin, for long-lasting suffering, and which consists of contraction, being subject to dissolution.
The ocean of the people of Bhītajana; the fear arising from its waters, or the wind that has the form of that [fear]; the crossing over it, which is the act of saving;
therein, the boats—those which are the supreme purifiers, exceedingly sacred.
Likewise, at the appropriate time— the morning— these cows, having been drawn by cowherds and being milked,
bestow joy upon the people with the streams of milk produced in the forenoon.
Scattered at the end of the day, they meet together in one place;
returning to the cow-pen, they experience the fear of existence arising from long-lasting suffering.

The meaning is that, by means of such giving and other virtues, they are like boats for crossing over the desert of saṃsāra, delivering one from the fear of worldly existence; thus, even their rays are supremely purifying. // 9 //
Out of devotion, those with their hands joined in *añjali* at the time of twilight bow their heads— the sole cause for the destruction of bondage— to [the Lord] out of devotion;
[this is] out of devotion.

May those rays of the sun, which bring awakening to the worlds like the beds of vast clusters of lotuses, and which are the wish-fulfilling trees for the expansive aspirations of your own minds, become for you the banners of the destruction of all defilement, free from conceptual construction. 10.

Those rays of the sun are like wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) for that great and vast prayer— which accords with the mind— of your own heart, which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and free from discursive thought (*nirvicāra*), and which possesses both breadth and loftiness.
May they awaken; may they come to be. Who are they?
Those who bring about awakening within the depths and in the midst of the vast expanses of lotus clusters—that is, of the multitudes of people in the world. In the case of the world:

Knowledge and awakening; in the case of the lotus, blossoming. Of what kind of people? "Upon their heads" means those by whom the twilight-folded palms (saṃdhyāñjali) have been bound with affection through prostration and salutation upon their heads. Of what kind of awakening?

They bind: in the case of the world, they are the sole cause for the destruction of the bondage of saṃsāra; in the case of the lotus, they are the cause for the removal of the binding of the enclosure of petals. Furthermore, of what nature are the rays of the sun?
They are the banners of *kalmaṣa*, that is, of sin, like the planet Ketu situated in an unfavorable position.
"Causing terror. According to Amara, *ketu* refers to a specific type of planet (*grahabheda*), and the term *abja* (and others) is used in the neuter when referring to a collection (*kadamba*).
In the second half of this verse, there is an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) on the letter *ka*. 10.

May those rays of the sun, in every way and without exception or doubt, serve as the banners—meaning the causes of destruction—of your impurity and sin. Of what nature are they? [They are] that which is inlaid...
By the greatness of the desire, "May this become vast for me," there is a most extensive and great prayer;
who are those givers, the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), of that prayer? They are those who [bestow] the vast realm of Bhojakhaṇḍa and Padmakhaṇḍa.

The phrase "as if it were her bed" is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). Having bowed their heads in devotion and prostrated themselves through diligent practice, those who have joined their palms in salutation at twilight—because of this very act, the people experience a sense of apprehension that they might be destroying a forest of lotuses; [the Lord is] the unique cause for the destruction of that very bondage, namely the bondage of worldly existence (saṃsāra-bandha).
They bring about the cause, awakening, and the knowledge of reality. // 10 //
In the calamity of poverty, the streams of water became instantly a hand of support against the precipice; in the calamity of poverty,
the streams of water [were] for the sake of wealth.

May the rays of the sun— the sole lamps illuminating sentient beings— protect you from defilement; for they act as gatekeepers at the threshold of the bodies of yogis striving for nirvāṇa as they set out toward the city of the Lord of the Third Heaven, and they bring the bliss of the dawn of day.
[May it protect] you from impurity,
or from dejection, [and from] the hot rays of the sun of intense heat.
May your rays protect you from *kaśmala*, that is, from delusion. Of what nature are they? They are "streams" (*dhārā*);
[they protect] in the calamity consisting of the thirst for wealth, which is greed.
The streams—that is, the flows—of wealth belonging to his own circle of devotees;

furthermore, of what nature were they? In the reading "prayāte" (when [the devotee] has set out), meaning upon a fall or stumble, they became instantly like supports for the hand—like ropes for grasping the hand. Furthermore...

Of what nature are they? "In truth": they are the primary lamps in the light, that is, the manifestation, of reality (*tattva*), which is the supreme Brahman as it truly is. Again, of what nature are they? "In heaven" (*tridiva*).

Indra is the lord of the third heaven; his city is heaven itself, and those [streets] are like the lines of paths leading toward it. Furthermore, how are they described? "Nirvāṇa..."—for those yogins who are diligent (*sodyama*) and striving toward *nirvāṇa*, that is, liberation (*mokṣa*), these are the supreme (*pragamam utkṛṣṭam*) [paths].
The place of departure, from which there is no return, is one's own body;

the solar orb acts as a cane-staff for that [body], behaving like a cane-staff—meaning it serves to ward off those who lack the authority to proceed there. Here, by the word "cane" (*vetra*), that [orb] is indicated through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the case of "the cane-bearers" (*vetradhara*) and so forth, they are called *vārikas* (gatekeepers), just as one says "the spears enter. Alternatively, those who possess canes are "cane-bearers" (*vetra*); the suffix *ac* is applied here because it belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group. Now, yogins are of two kinds.

Some desire supernatural powers (*siddhi*), while others desire liberation (*mukti*). Having first attained a divine body through the power of yoga, they wander at will among the worlds, enjoying sensory pleasures. Due to their negligence, they may at some point again become attached to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Birth, death, and so forth occur; however, those [beings] are unable to reach the solar disk. But those who are intent upon *nirvāṇa* proceed to liberation by way of the solar disk. Furthermore, what are these rays like? They are "pleasant at the beginning of the day," that is, at the start of the day.

They are pleasant (*sukhāḥ*) because they possess warmth and because they do not obstruct rain, thus producing happiness. Now, since it has been stated that within the three substances there exist demerit (*pāpa*), merit (*puṇya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth, the word "pleasure" (*sukha*) does not denote a substance.

The word takes the gender of its referent (*vācyaliṅgatvam*). As for the derivation from the word itself, in the sense of "producing happiness," one forms *sukhā* by adding the suffix *ac* (specifically *aṇ*) to the word *sukha*, as in the case of *citadatta*. Or, [it may be derived] from *kalmaṣa*.

This reading, however, should be disregarded because it disrupts the alliteration (*anuprāsa*). According to Amara, *garddha* means "greed for wealth. Regarding the word *pragama*: by relying on some etymological derivation (*saṃjñā*) in whatever way possible, it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), according to the rule *puṃsi saṃjñāyām*.

Or rather, by relying on the meaning that "kṛtyas" refers to all *kṛt* suffixes in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the word "gama" is included even in the governing rule *grahabṛhanniścigamaśca* which pertains to the locative case.

When [the suffix] *siddha* is established, there is the superior understanding (*pragama*). The term *pragama* is a *prādi*-compound. In this regard, some have split the word *adhanāya* in the manuscript and added the marginal note *āpādya nirdhanāya rāyodhārā*; however, that [interpretation] belongs to the dative case (*caturthī*).
Because it is incapable [of producing knowledge] and because its root is ignorance of words, the notion of *dhana* is disregarded. 11.

May the rays of the intensely radiant sun protect you— may they guard you from distress (or, according to an alternative reading, from defilement)— what kind of rays? Those which take the form of streams of wealth for the one who is without wealth, the destitute.
They are givers of much;
in times of calamity and misfortune, they instantly and immediately become a forest of arms [to protect] against the precipice.
They are illuminators for sentient beings—living creatures—and are uncommon lamps in the light of reality (*tattva-āloka*). (In the reading *tatvāloke*, it refers to the light of reality.)

The light of Brahman is of that very nature; the meaning is that they are like a single lamp. On the departure for the city of Tridivapati, Indra—that is, upon going to heaven—they are indeed like streets or paths that produce heaven. Those who are diligent in *nirvāṇa*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*).
The entry of those yogins into such a place [as this] was like using the word *vetra* (staff) for a doorkeeper (*pratihāra*)—
that is, acting metaphorically;
they were performing the expulsion of unwelcome people by means of their own bodies as if they were staffs.
For those who are capable and equal to them—namely, the yogis—go to Brahman after piercing the solar orb;
as it has been said:
"There are only two persons in this world who pierce the solar orb."
The wandering mendicant (parivrāj) engaged in yoga, moving toward his destination, was struck at the beginning of the day;
likewise, those who possess the nature of happiness find happiness at the start of the day. 11.

In the east, moving forward not long ago, they placed their beautiful crest-jewels upon the mountain as if to abundantly smear the faces of the quarters with liquid yellow pigment for their lofty adornment;
they were being honored by the steady glances of the cakravāka birds with clever words of endearment.
With speech that is charming and unwavering.
May the rays of the fierce sun, which are the most excellent among all things contemplated, perform what is appropriate for you. 12.

May the rays of the sun— the non-final, primordial splendors of Caṇḍarocis— act in such a way as to be appropriate and fitting for those things desired and longed for, so that the objects of one's longing may be attained.

May they engage in giving. Of what sort? On the eastern mountain, the eastern peak, they have for a short time—not for a long duration—performed the role of the crest-jewel, the excellent head-ornament.

Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are as if pouring forth, or casting upward, abundant *rocanāmbu*—saffron water—for the purpose of anointing (*carcanāya*) or sprinkling (*secanāya*) the quarters, which are like brides of the directions. Furthermore, of what nature are they? By means of *cāṭuktaiḥ*—flattering words—to those whose hearts are bent toward [the Lord].

Being honored with respectful words of endearment and clever, steady, and unwavering glances— eyes capable of dispelling the pain of their mutual separation caused by the night— they were thus venerated with devotion.

The meaning is that they are being gazed upon with respect, preceded by pleasant words. In the compound *caṇḍarocīrucaḥ*, since it is a genitive tatpuruṣa, the *r* is elided by the rule *rori*, and then the vowel is lengthened by the rule *ḍhralopaḥ*.
Here, there is an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) on the letter *c*. //12//
"Prācī" refers to the rays of the sun, which are like fierce light; they release for you the water of radiance.
Of what nature are they? At dawn, on the eastern mountain—the mountain of sunrise—for not very long, that is, for a short time.
In whatever manner they act as crest-jewels— that is,
as ornaments for the head— they emit abundant drops of liquid *rocanā* in such a way that they serve as a frequent object of intense contemplation and grasping for the quarters of the sky.

As if being honored with clever, affectionate words spoken by the eyes of the *cakravāka* birds—which are unwavering and motionless—the [sages], who are themselves non-final (*acarama*), [behold the Lord].
For at night, due to separation from their beloveds, the *cakravākas* gaze upon the Blessed One with great reverence. They are not final.
The ancients. 12.
One light for you is the sun; two are your eyes; three are spoken of by the lotus-faced Brahmā as the worlds; four are the elements;
