five are the senses; likewise, six are the various kinds found in the six seasons;
seven are those praised by the gods and sages; and eight are the quarters of space—may these rays of yours, O Sun, [grant us prosperity].
May the hundreds of rays of light, which at dawn attain the state of nine by losing one, bestow auspiciousness upon us. 13.
May those thousand rays of the Sun grant you auspiciousness; which ones? Those which existed prior to creation.

The light is one, being of the nature of the splendor of the Supreme Brahman; this is a metaphorical description. Likewise, hereafter, regarding the Lord who has assumed the form of the Virāṭ after the subsequent creation, his eyes are seen in the form of the sun and the moon. Furthermore, of what kind are they? They are such that [they illuminate] the three worlds.

The collection of the three worlds is the *trijagat* (the triple world), also known as the *trilokī*. Therein, those praises were sung by the four lotus-born faces—that is, by the mouths of Brahmā, who was born from the lotus in the navel of the Blessed One. Furthermore, [those praises] which [were uttered] by the five elements...

Among earth, water, air, space, and fire, the fifth is fire; its forms are as follows: likewise, those various kinds of cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth that occur excessively during the six seasons are indeed the rays of the sun in the form of seasonal phenomena.
"They transform," according to the ancient saying. Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Seven.
For the sake of the seven, they are praised—that is, lauded—by the thirty gods and the sages, namely the celestial seers (devarṣis) and the seven seers (saptarṣis). Again, of what nature are they?

"Aṣṭadigbhāñji" means they partake of the eight directions; that is to say, they extend everywhere in succession. Furthermore, in the forenoon (*prāhṇe*), they attain "novelty" (*navatvam*)—meaning freshness—or, in another sense, the state of being nine in number. This is due to their being devoid of increase or decrease.

The meaning is that even those things which are of the nature of doubt appear as if newly arisen in the morning due to worldly convention; here, the word "yānti" ends in a present participial suffix (*śatṛ*).
The exposition up to ten by means of the sequence of commencement is skillfulness. 13.
"One": may those one thousand rays of the sun grant you auspiciousness and welfare. Of what nature are they? At dawn, they attain "newness"—that is, freshness and the state of being nine in number.
Those which occupy the eight directions— meaning those existing in the eight cardinal points and established as the eight principles to be realized by yogis—
and which have been praised and lauded by the seven celestial sages (deva-ṛṣis).
Which are they?
Those which are the one light and illumination in the three worlds— that is, in the entire collection of the three realms— and the two eyes.
Those [qualities] which were uttered and praised by the four lotus-born faces of Brahmā,
as well as the fifth form of the elements— earth and so forth— which is of the nature of splendor, and likewise among the six sacrifices;
Enough with this excessive elaboration;
the various types of numerical relations are to be understood everywhere in this manner. //13//
With their entire worlds whirling in confusion, they bear as it were exhaustion, being parched by their own heat;
all [the worlds].
Like those scorched by a forest fire in summer, they repeatedly suck the essence from the earth;
[scorched by a forest fire]. Scorched by a forest fire.
O Earth,
you vomited forth your waters during the rainy season as if from the affliction of excessive heat, and [now] in the winter season...
May the non-fierce rays of Mārtaṇḍa long be for the destruction of your misfortune. 14.
May they be; may they belong to you.
May the rays—the reins—of Mārtaṇḍa long be for your destruction of inauspiciousness, that is, for the cutting away of misfortune.
Of what nature are they? They are "āvṛtti-," meaning they have repeatedly (āvṛttyā) traversed the wandering mind.

Those by whom the entire world was [traversed] are thus; for that very reason, they appear as if bearing the fatigue born of wandering on the path. Furthermore, they are dried up by their own heat—that is, the heat produced by their own exhaustion. Sañjāta.
As if their hearts, palates, and mouths were parched;
as if scorched by a forest fire; as if heated by the fires of a desert on the middle path; those who repeatedly and incessantly suck and drink the sap of the earth during the summer.

"Punarāttā" means taken up again; that is, they were swallowed with excessive greed in the form of vomiting and such. During the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*), they vomited out the water they had drunk; then, during the winter season (*hemanta*), they were not fierce [in their thirst] once again.
They are weak. Here too, the word "iva" (as if) is to be connected; or rather, this is a case of an elliptical poetic fancy (*luptotprekṣā*). The meaning is as follows:
such is the worldly order that a traveler who constantly moves day and night becomes filled with satisfaction by the heat born of the exhaustion of the road and the heat of the forest fire.

He drinks water excessively; because of that, the disease of vomiting arises in him, and afflicted by it, he becomes emaciated. Having observed the condition of the world, the poet has summarized this and expressed it through a particular stylistic turn of phrase.
A hymn of praise is indeed offered to Sūryābhībhuṣaṇā: having gathered all essence during the eight months, she pours it forth without restraint in the rainy season.

The intended meaning is that they discharge [these rays]. Their majesty is renowned for curing all diseases that are otherwise incurable. These rays are indeed fierce like the sun's beams; however, during the winter season, because they travel far due to the sun being in its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), there is an excess of cold.
"They were perceived by the people as if they were not fierce. Regarding the word *abhīṣu*, Amara states: "It means a rein or a rope. (14)

Regarding the word "āvṛtti" (return): here, the word "eva" (indeed) is used everywhere to indicate a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). During the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*), the waters were swallowed by those [clouds] who had contracted a disease caused by excessive drinking; thus, in the winter season (*hemanta*), they vomited forth water that was not fierce but mild, like the rays of the sun.
O rays, may your showers be for the long-term destruction of inauspiciousness—the eradication of the sins accumulated over many births.
Which ones? Those that repeatedly suck the essence of the earth during the summer heat; what are they like? As if scorched by a forest fire. (By way of ellipsis: [May they be so for us.]

By their revolving and wandering, the universe has been set in motion; for this very reason, they appear as if bearing weariness, as if carrying it, and by their own heat, as if parching, that is to say, as if possessing dryness. //14//

Indeed, for the brides of the quarters, the mere sky alone— beautified by a tawny hue arising from a slight touch of the deep redness of their state, which is lovely with an exceedingly sweet radiance—
is sufficient.

May the thousand rays of the Sun, the Lord of Dharma, grant you prosperity— those rays which, at the onset of day, possess the splendor of blossoming lotus eyes and appear like a row of beard-stubble just beginning to emerge. 15.

May the thousandfold radiance of the sun, the heat-rayed one, bestow protection upon you; herein he utters a poetic conceit: like what? Like the light of the dawn as it is slightly breaking forth at the beginning of the day.
Becoming manifest like a row of facial hair in the quarters of the sky,
he describes the emergence of youth by attributing the state of a bridegroom to the day and the state of a leader to that [day].
What kind of row of beards is it?
It is that of the "brides of the directions"; that is, of the brides who are the personified quarters of the sky.
This [light] is exceedingly sweet;
its appearance and its radiance at the onset of day extend a state of loveliness to the quarters, who are like brides— this is the sense of the genitive case.
This is to be construed with the phrase "exceedingly sweet. The stage when a beard first appears on the faces of young men produces even greater affection in brides.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Climbed," etc.
One who has ascended, that is, one who has reached [it].

A slight degree of maturity (*prauḍhileśa*) is a small amount of fullness; by that, the row of whiskers (*śmaśruśreṇī*), having attained a tawny hue (*kapilimā*)— that is, a reddish-brown color— is supported or sustained at the time of its first emergence due to a little maturity.
That she was born with a tawny complexion is established by experience. Furthermore, of what kind was she?
She was one whose ornamentation of the face—consisting solely of its natural adornment—was manifested through the growth of a beard, independent of all other [artificial] ornaments.
An extraordinary natural splendor arises at the onset of youth. At what kind of dawn? At that dawn in which there is the radiance of eyes, which are actually blossoming lotuses (*ambuja*).
Just as there is an excellence of beauty in the eyes of a youth at the commencement of youth, so too is there such splendor here.
There is a resemblance to a blooming lotus. Here, by means of this mode of praise expressed through a turn of phrase (*vacobhaṅgī*),
the unmentioned erotic sentiment (*aprastuta-śṛṅgāra-rasa*) flows forth for the nourishment of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

"Cāturyam" [is derived as follows]: "daśaśatī" means a collection of ten hundreds; because it is a *dvigu* compound ending in a short vowel, and because such a *dvigu* is feminine according to the rule "dvigoḥ," [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied].
The suffix *ṅīp* is established [here]. According to Amara: "Tanūruha, roma, and loma denote body hair; śmaśru denotes the beard on a man's face."
May the thousandfold collection of rays— the beams of light— of the sun, whose splendor is heat, grant you *śarma*, that is, happiness;
for Amara states that *śarma* means peace and happiness.

Of what nature was it? At that dawn— the face of day in which the splendor of the lotus-like eye was blossoming and expanding— this [splendor] may be imagined as a row of beard-threads slightly emerging.

The quarters themselves are the women; the light that shines forth from them is exceedingly sweet. Spreading a delightful state through that radiance, she is adorned with the beauty of a tawny hue, which has emerged and been sustained by a touch of full maturity.
From that very moment, as soon as they emerge,
they become full-grown tawny ones in an instant; even their rows of beard bloom like eyes upon a blossoming lotus.

Her radiance, emerging slightly upon her face wherever it may be, spreads a delightful state of being—like the sight of a flash of light—that is exceedingly sweet and charming for young women; she is one who is adorned by that [radiance] which has blossomed forth through a slight ascent of its intensity. // 15 //
He who, as if apprehensive, was deprived by the bull-bannered Lord of the luster of his crest-jewel—
that very luster which was taken away by the bull-bannered one.

He was sufficiently praised by Kṛṣṇa— who, as if terrified of being surpassed by his own body which was dark as the gloom— by that Lord who dwells within the hollow cave of the interior of a lotus just opened at dawn.
May even the thinnest emergence of the rays of the enemy of darkness be for your protection, like the moon. 16.
The emergence of the rays of the sun,
the enemy of darkness; though extremely subtle and thin, it has arisen in the morning as an emergence of rays.
May there be the emergence,
the rising, of splendors; may there be protection for garments.
By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even the most minute," the inferiority of luminous bodies is also observed.
From this statement, even his [the sun's] capacity for protection is revealed. Of what kind is the rising?
It is "maulī" (crowned). He is exceedingly praised by Rudra, who has the bull as his mark. By whom? By this Blessed Sun, who is mine...
"May it not steal—
may it not take away— the splendor of the moon situated in the sky," [he thought] as if possessed by apprehension.

The meaning is: "He acted as if possessed by fear, thinking, 'May he not steal [me] who am situated upon the crown of his head,' just as one who has been robbed [fears further loss]. Furthermore, he who was created by the Creator...

He was praised by Brahmā. With what kind [of praise]? "With one that is fresh," and so forth. "Fresh" means new, having been opened at that very moment; the "hollow" refers to the interior of that lotus, his own seat.
Because of its depth, it is like a cave; since Brahmā is situated within it as if in a cave, he is difficult to perceive at night due to the closing of the lotus.
He is praised for his beneficence, as he becomes well-situated when the lotus opens at sunrise. Furthermore...

Of what kind [is he]? He is praised by Kṛṣṇa—that is, by Viṣṇu. By what kind [of Viṣṇu]? By one who is terrified of the humiliation of his own body, which, like darkness (dhvānta), has been drawn forth (kṛṣṭi).

"By the one who is afraid in the darkness" means by one who is terrified that the Lord Sun, being provoked to anger, might likewise humiliate him; for here, because the illustrious Sūryanārāyaṇa is the object of worship for all, his praise is performed at the twilight (sandhyā) by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

This is the actual meaning. However, by means of poetic ingenuity, the poet has described the praise of Viṣṇu and Rudra as being caused by fear, whereas that of Brahmā is caused by joy. In the word *trastaḥ*, the suffix *kta* is applied according to the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ*. // 16 //

May the emergence of the rays of the enemy of darkness—the Sun—though exceedingly slight (*tanīyān*), be for your protection. He who was praised by Śiva, the bull-bannered one (*vṛṣabhāṅka*), thinking, "Is this [emergence] from the moon on my crest (*maulīnduḥ*)?"—thus [it was said]. What is this emergence of rays? [It is from the moon on his crest.]
He was praised by the Creator (Brahmā), who, fearing that the moon’s splendor might steal away or destroy the luster of his own head-crest,
seemed to remain within the hollows and caves— the inner regions— of the freshly blossomed lotus,
as if to protect it from the darkness-like blackness [of the moon].
The meaning is that Nārāyaṇa was not sufficiently praised by Kṛṣṇa, who, as if terrified by the humiliation of his own body [as a boar] at her hands, offered excessive praise. 16.
Those by whom the vast sky, the ten long quarters, and the earth— with its mountains, cities, and the expanse of its forests— are suddenly made visible as the oceans have their tides dispersed;
and by whom the lotus-beds are awakened at dawn after they have destroyed the darkness of the world.
May the thousand-rayed ones swiftly cause that which is disagreeable to you to fall away. 17.
The rays— the morning beams— of you, who possess a thousand splendors and a thousand rays, [shall quickly and swiftly bring] that which is undesirable and unpleasant to you.
Let them cause [it] to slacken;
let them cast it far away. Who are they? Those by whom the dark night of ignorance has been destroyed.

The lotus-pond revives the world as well; the meaning is that it is rescued and comforted, as if from the prison of the dense darkness of night. By what means? By those [rays] by which the sky was contracted with darkness.
By those making it vast through the rejection of that [limit],
and likewise suddenly making the ten directions long;
by those whose ocean waters have their tides cast away— that is, whose boundary waters have been driven far off.
By those [waves] making [the shore resound];
at midnight, the waters of the oceans—the seas—spread across their shores with surging billows; in the morning, the rays of the sun [dry] them.
Having dried up the shores of the oceans, they reveal them. Furthermore, by what means? "By being visible" (dṛśyaiḥ);
that is, because the darkness that veiled the earth has vanished, the expanse of mountains—meaning peaks—cities, and *nagas*, meaning trees, becomes capable of being seen.
By them, [the earth] was made complete, filling the vast earth;
for Amara states: "naga and aga denote both mountain and tree. (nagāvagau = śailavṛkṣau). Naga and aga refer to mountains and trees. Naga and aga.
Ābhoga means fullness; thus also says Amara. 17.
"Extensive" means this: may those rays of the thousand-rayed sun—the *usra*s—loosen for you (*vaḥ*) the sin that is undesirable to you.
Which ones? Those by which the lotus-pond is awakened at dawn (*uṣasi*), [that is,] from the dark night (*tamisrā*), the night belonging to darkness (*tāmasī*).

Having destroyed even the world, it is being uplifted and illuminated. By what means? By those [rays] which, at the rising of the moon, cause the darkness to vanish across the expanse of the sky; by those whose splendors cause the oceans to overflow their shores; and by those [rays] which illuminate the world along with all its beings.
It is being uplifted, that is, it is being made manifest.

By what means? By those which, as they expand across the sky, cause the darkness to depart; whose seals [the ocean shores] have their tides dispersed, and who thus become full of joy at the rising of the sun. And at sunrise...

Instantly, at that very moment, they made all the ten directions full of water; the mountains, the peaks, and the cities appeared as if the entire earth, the bearer of wealth, had been stretched out long.
And by those trees, through their expanse— that is, their width— they made the earth vast; therefore,
in relation to space and time, it is the eastern direction, and in relation to the time of dawn, it is the eastern quarter belonging to Indra (Śatakratu),
known as Nānānaga.
In the reading "pāṭhe dṛśyamānatvam," the term "nagādi" (mountains and so forth) is the qualifier; in the reading "dṛśyanānānaga," both [terms] are indeed qualifiers of that [subject]. // 17 //
Devoid of confusion and emptiness, possessing innate brilliance and imperishability,
he who— though situated in a single location— is capable of dispelling darkness throughout the entire universe like a lamp within a room; he alone,
by virtue of his relation to space and time, bears the title of "New" for the sun as it traverses the three worlds.
May that rising of rays which has gone toward the direction of Śatakratu bestow auspiciousness upon you. 18.
He who has gone;
he who is going, [before] the hot-rayed sun of sharp brilliance.
May that source, the rising of rays— that is, of lights— grant you auspiciousness.
Who is he? He who is capable of making the entire world free from obstructing darkness—that is, dispelling all obscurity.
Who is like what? Like a lamp in a house. Of what nature is he? Even though situated in a single location.
It remains fixed in a specific location within the space of the sky. By the word "even," it indicates its distinction from other lamps;
for that lamp sometimes stays inside and sometimes outside the lamp-stand or in the hand, remaining in various locations, whereas this [light] is constant, whether to the south or to the north.

It occupies the space of the sky; by that very [space], it moves and dispels the darkness of the three worlds. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is empty of being either extinguished or scattered. That [ordinary fire] is extinguished (*asta*) by the wind, while "scattered" (*vyasta*) means it is not moved even by a gentle breeze as it drifts here and there. This [light], however, proceeds to another continent.
Because it is beyond the range of worldly vision, it appears as if it has set, though not in reality. Furthermore, of what nature is it?

It possesses its own luster and is eternally radiant, yet during the day it is devoid of light. Again, of what nature is it? "Aniśam" means that while it is imperishable day and night, it is extinguished due to the absence of oil and a wick. Again, of what nature is it?

In the eastern direction belonging to Śatakratu—that is, connected with Indra—the ancient one, though having first appeared in the east, attained the name "Nava" (the New); although he is established by people as "Nava," he is made new every single day. Of what sort [is he]?

"Of the one with sharp rays"? [The answer is] "of the directions. This refers to the one who, out of a desire to produce distinctions among the directions—such as east and so forth—and among times—such as morning and so forth—for the sake of benefiting others, wanders through the three worlds without dependence on them; for the Agnihotra and other rites would be impossible for one who is not delimited by direction, time, and the like.
The meaning is constant wandering for the purpose of setting forth the path of Dharma. Regarding the word *svaka*, Amara states: "In the three genders, *svaka* means one's own (*nitya*). // 18 //
"So be it. May this emergence of the rays of the sun, who wanders and traverses the three worlds, bestow—grant—auspiciousness (*śiva*) unto you.
Of what nature is he? With respect to space and time, he is the eastern direction.

With respect to the time of dawn, he has gone—that is, proceeded—to that which is called "the new" (nava) in the eastern direction belonging to Śatakratu; this is what is meant by "the new. Who is this? It is the rising of the first rays of light.

Even though situated in one place—that is, occupying only a single spot—he is capable (īśaḥ), meaning empowered, to make the entire universe free from darkness; just as a lamp, even while remaining in one location, is capable of making a house free from darkness, so it is here. He then states the distinction [of the Lord] from that [lamp]:

Let this fire, though extremely feeble, be one that is not lacking its own radiance—being devoid of both "asta" (destruction) and "dhvaṃsa" (dispersion), and thus free from agitation. It is a fire whose luster does not perish during the day (aniśāyām), whereas the light of a lamp perishes day and night; it is imperishable.
This is the meaning. // 18 //

He who shines upon the side of the world-and-non-world not merely for the sake of that which is designated by that name—
him alone [I worship].

May that mass of light, which dispels the darkness, protect you—that mass whose length is abandoned for fear of shattering the upper shell of the cosmic egg, and whose limit is the very space of the sky, subject as it is to its own will. 19.
The obstruction of light;
that is the obstruction of light.
May the well-known mass of radiance belonging to Tapanas, the Sun, protect you. Who is he? [He is the one] from whom [darkness] has departed.
The lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*) is a slender fiber; "mṛṇālī" refers to that same thing.
This world of the Nāgas is soft and delicate; [he thought] out of compassion alone, "May it not wither—that is, may it not suffer from my heat. May it not come to such a state.
For he who has not entered the world does not shine upon the further side of the mountain Lokāloka— that is,
for the sake of its meaning and for the sake of protecting its name— even though the Creator gave it the name "Lokāloka" for another purpose.
It was made for that mountain so that if the glorious sun were to scorch even its opposite side, the boundary established by the Creator would be violated;
thus, it was for the purpose of protecting it. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is upright.
The meaning is that he has abandoned his length out of fear of the bursting or splitting of that portion of the cosmic egg which is its upper part.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? "At the limit of heaven" (dyusīmni); that is, in the region of space (ākāśadeśe).
"One whose limit of movement is determined by his own will" means that although he is capable of moving everywhere at his own pleasure,
out of compassion he moves only within a restricted area; such is the meaning.
"Ogha" refers to a multitude or the current of water, according to Amara;
"mṛṇāla" and "bisam" also mean the lotus stalk. Furthermore, the word "strī" may be used for things like the *mṛṇālī* when there is a desire to express diminution. // 19 //

The far side of the mountain Lokāloka conveys its name precisely for the sake of preserving that etymological significance; it does not at all suggest anything else. For if there were light even there, then it would indeed be *loka* (the world) and not *aloka* (non-world); such is the conclusion.

At the summit, reaching to the very limit of the sky at the top of the cosmic egg, he is one whose height is abandoned by both [sides] because of that bursting forth; thus, it means he is the boundary of the expanse of space, which is subject to his own will and under his control. // 19 //
When he rises, the world does not become dark even for a moment, nor does the moon, though its rays are cool as frost, immediately undergo waning; indeed,
there is no bondage for those with palms joined in reverence, nor even for the grove of night-lotuses.
May that light of the sun, which is to be beheld at dawn and which exceeds all desires, grant you [fulfillment]. 20.
May that light, the splendor of the Lord of Day, grant you objects of desire exceeding even your wildest aspirations. What is it? It is that which, as it rises—
When he is rising, the single, solitary time—the morning hour—is not dark;
rather, even the time at the end of the world is not dark. For while the night is dark, the end of the world is not dark, but radiant.
Of what nature is it? It is free from darkness, meaning that darkness has departed from it. Furthermore, it is the "Prāleyapāda," the mountain whose foothills consist of snow.
The Himalaya alone does not immediately undergo dissolution; however, even the moon— the "Himalaya"—
undergoes dissolution, melting due to its connection with the heat of the sun.
The moon, however, has gone to its dissolution and set; yet for the *siddhāñjalis* there is no single bond of affection.
Rather, even for the *siddhāñjalis* of the night-lotus grove, there is a union for the purpose of saluting at twilight.

But there is a connection with the petals of the lily grove. Therefore, what kind of splendor is it? It is "at dawn"; because of its tenderness at the time of dawn, it is "prekṣaṇīya," meaning it is capable of being seen.

And [the word] *ujjihāna* means "delightful. It is a form derived from the root *ohāṅ* in the sense of "going" with the suffix *śānac*. According to the *Anekārthakośa*, a woman sixteen years of age is called *śyāmā*, as is the night; thus it has multiple meanings.
"May that splendor—the light of the Lord of Day (the Sun), which is to be beheld at dawn—grant you desires exceeding even your wildest hopes. What is it?
It is that unique blackness which appears when [the sun] is rising."

He does not become bright or composed; rather, even the end of the world becomes free from darkness, non-black, and composed instantly, at that very moment. And he who has frost upon his feet, though possessing redness, does not merely undergo dissolution—that is, melting—but furthermore—

Even the moon undergoes dissolution and withering for the sake of saluting the sun; for the twilight salutations with joined palms are indeed not merely a bond for the moon, but also the cause of the contraction of the grove of night-lotuses. 20.
That which does not steal the luster of lotuses but rather makes them more beautiful;

which does not possess the brilliance of stars but utterly eclipses them instantly; and which is unable to close its eyes for even a moment, let alone for a day—that one thing alone [is the cause] of the three worlds.
May that eye, which is unlike the common eye of the sun, be for your great glory.

May that great splendor of the Radiant One be for you—the destroyer of evil (*aghabhit*), meaning the dispeller of sin, suffering, and calamity. Of what nature is it? It is the one, unique eye of the three worlds, illuminating all objects. What kind of eye is it?
The other [lotuses] are common, whereas the eye is dissimilar to them—that is, it is of a different kind. He expresses this very dissimilarity with the word "yat" (which):
that which does not steal away the splendor of the lotuses; on the contrary, by way of contrast, it possesses a superior beauty.

The other eye, however, steals away the beauty of the lotuses with its own splendor; furthermore, it does not bear nor does it nourish the luster of the stars—that is, the brilliance of the constellations—but rather constantly veils and obscures them with tears. As for that [other eye]...

It bears, nourishes, or maintains the luster of a star, the beauty of the pupil; furthermore, it is not merely unable or incapable of closing for a short duration (nimeṣa), but is capable of doing so even for a whole day. That indeed—
It is capable of nothing other than the mere closing of its eyes.
Furthermore, of what kind is that one, the peerless? It is the four-faced and five-faced one.
For those with six faces and so forth, [the number] follows their respective number of faces; for others, however, it is two-fold.
According to Amara, the *kanīnikā* is the pupil of the eye (*tārakākṣṇaḥ*).
"Alas! Suffering! Calamity! Sin!"—thus [he cries]. //21//
"That which"—it is that which is unlike and distinct from the common eye of the three worlds;
may that great splendor (*mahas*) of the Radiant One (*bhāsvat*) be for you (*vaḥ*), O destroyers of misfortune (*maghabhit*), a destroyer of sins.
What is it? That which steals away the luster of the lotuses, and conversely, [bestows it upon them].
It bestows upon them an exceedingly beautiful luster; it steals away the common splendor of lotuses by its very likeness,
yet it does not even strive for the radiance of the stars.
The ordinary eye utterly obscures— that is, eclipses— the light of the pupil;
for while the ordinary eye is not merely unable to constantly efface it but is even capable of making it day,
the ordinary eye itself [is surpassed by that which] makes day.
The meaning is that what is capable of performing even a single blink of an eye is not capable [of doing so] when it is two; thus, there is a distinction between them. //21//

As if out of a thirst for the touch of the exceedingly cool surface of the water of the night, the quarters of space quickly abandoned the earth and, as if out of compassion, swiftly leaped over even the foot of Viṣṇu to reach the far distance, like the trunks of elephants reaching for the lotuses in a lake.
May the intensely radiant splendor of the Sun, shining forth, consume all ill omens for you. 22.
It would be unrestrained; it would be the unrestrained splendor of the sun.
May [the fire] burn—that is, reduce to ashes—the evil omens of the morning, such as bad dreams and the like; for it is fitting that fire should reduce things to ashes. Of what nature is its radiance?
It is "unrestrained" (uddāma); that is, it is unrestrained (unobstructed) and shining.
And: "pervading the three worlds"—here she imagines in many ways.

Regarding the word *kṣmām*: the surface of the earth (*tala*) is the ground; it is exceedingly cool because of the nocturnal water—the dew fallen at night—and from the thirst or longing for the touch of that [surface], she descends more swiftly—*kṣepīyaḥ*, meaning more quickly.

Just as if her voice had reached this divine earth, *kṣmā-pṛthvī*— this being a form of the root *rug*, meaning "to go"— as if for the sake of cooling it due to its extreme heat; furthermore, the quarters (*āśā*) and their elephants (*dvirada*).
The world-elephants (diggajas) are their prisons, and those very oceans are their lotuses;
as if to lead them quickly and swiftly to awakening—that is, to full expansion—the quarters of space resounded with the roar of the sun’s radiance. [The word] "puṣkara" is to be applied here as well.
Because its nature is that of awakening (*vodhana*), there too exists the *puṣkara*. Here, *puṣkaras* refers to the tips of the trunks of elephants;

for the lexicon states: "*Puṣkara* [denotes] the tip of an elephant's trunk, a musical instrument, water, the sky, the blade of a sword, a lotus, a sacred ford, and a specific medicinal herb. Furthermore, of what kind is she? [She is] Viṣṇu’s...

He avoids the footprint out of revulsion or with extreme haste; having leaped over it from afar, he does so because the footprint of the worshipful Viṣṇu, situated at a great distance, is not to be trodden upon by feet—meaning he avoids it out of a sense of dharma-revulsion. Here, "the footprint of Viṣṇu" [is mentioned].
"Vyoma" [is used] because of the synonymy "viyat" and "viṣṇupada";
"ghṛṇā" means "jugupsā" and "karuṇā," according to Amara.

The form *kṣepīyaḥ* is established in the sense of "extremely swift" through the application of the suffix *īyasun* according to the rule *sthūladūrayuvahasvakṣiprakṣudrāṇāṃ yaṇādiparaṃ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ*, which effects the replacement of the initial consonant with *yaṇ* and the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel for the preceding one. Similarly, *daviyasī* is established in the sense of "extremely distant" by the same process. In this context, [the suffix] *tarap* and so forth are applied by that [same rule].

The reading [is as follows]: "sādhīyān" is better because the word *ṛta*, when conventionally established in the sense of "truth," is not misleading; the meaning "attained from here" (*itā prāptā*) is easily understood. //22//

"Kṣmāmi" means: may the radiance of the Lord of Day burn away your ill-omened dreams, that which produces suffering, or your sin. Of what nature is it? It is that which is more cooling—more cool than the surface of the waters of the night—which is the very bottom, the lowest depth.
Then, as if out of longing for the other spies, she went to the earth; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). Likewise hereafter:
the trunks of the elephants of the quarters (the world-elephants) are themselves the lakes or lotus-pools, and [she went there] to the lotuses.

As if to lead them suddenly and instantly toward awakening and expansion, at that very moment of dawn when the distant Sindhu had reached its destination, she— shining intensely as if to censure Viṣṇu’s abode, the sky, for being so easily transgressed by his excessive speed, saying "Viṣṇu’s abode is thus to be overstepped"— spread forth.
This is the meaning. // 22 //
She is not accessible even to the mountain that trembles with the force of the wind at the end of an eon,
nor even to the mountain that trembles with the force of the thunderbolt;
she is not accessible even to the one who possesses lips that surpass the earth.

May that very radiance of the lamp of all islands bring you joy—a radiance whose brilliant splendor was intensely emitted during the day, yet was not obscured by the collyrium of darkness; which attained its birth from the sun, yet did not undergo extinction; and which, though having changed its form, remains the same. 23.
May the radiance of the heat-light of the lamp of all islands— which, like a lamp, illuminates them— bring you happiness and dispel the darkness of ignorance.
By means of negation;
of what kind? Of another form, distinct from the light of other lamps.
He states this very distinction through qualifiers:
"No," [he replied].
"Cruel and merciless; by the fierce force of his arrows, the mountains—those bearers of the earth—are being shattered and destroyed. Even of such a one as this..."

The destruction of an eon and the end of an eon—that wind is unable to reach or overcome it; yet the flame of a lamp is extinguished by even a slight breeze. Furthermore, during the day, it is intensely, utterly, and brilliantly manifested.

She who possesses beauty (*śrī*) is [usually] one whose splendor is dull during the day; yet she is not devoid of darkness—that is, the darkness in the form of collyrium (*kajjala*). However, this is not the case.
But she, though devoid [of it], was indeed accompanied by collyrium; moreover, she was one whose birth was obtained from the *pataṅga* (the sun),
and who likewise underwent concealment (*moṣa*) or disappearance.
It has not gone;
rather, it suffers plunder from the *pataṅga*, a specific kind of minute bird, by which it is extinguished.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
*Avarttiḥ* means "without a wick" (*vartirahitā*), yet it remains supported by a wick;
*pataṅgau* refers to both a bird and the sun, according to Amara. // 23 //

It does not conceive [of itself as such]. May that radiance of the illuminating lamp—the heat-light of all those continents—whose form is otherwise and whose flame is distinct, bring you happiness; may it make you happy. Elsewhere...
She becomes the wick of the lamp; then he states her distinction: who is she? She who is not reachable, not attainable, by the wind of the end of the eon—the wind of dissolution—of what kind?
Of that very wind by which even the mountains are shattered by its merciless force, she is the wick, yet she is reachable and capable of being overcome by that wind.

She whose radiant beauty is deeply engraved during the day is not "deprived of darkness" (tamas) as if it were lampblack; rather, she is indeed devoid of it. But the wick (*varti*), whose bright splendor is deeply engraved during the day, is not "devoid of a mass of darkness" (*tamaḥ-kajjala*); on the contrary, it is possessed of it. Having obtained its origin from the *pataṅga*—the sun—it undergoes further theft [of light].
The wick has not met its destruction, nor has the moth fallen from the firefly; for according to Amara, "pataṅga" refers both to a bird and to the sun. // 23 //

Her nature is praiseworthy for its preeminent and weighty virtues that completely fill all desires; she remains fully risen on the mountain of dawn, lofty even during the slight dimming of the day’s departure.
She is utterly incapable of dwelling for even a moment in the same place as darkness.
May the kindled splendor of the Sun be like a brilliant light for you; may there be splendor for this object to be attained. 24.
May this blazing radiance of the Sun— his splendor— be for the attainment and acquisition of that which is desired and cherished; like the desire of a magnanimous lord.

It is equal to the sun’s own will. For the will of a magnanimous lord bestows upon the petitioner whatever object is desired. Of what nature is that splendor? It is "complete" (niḥśeṣā); [it is] of all things...

It is the filling of all hopes and directions; it is that which possesses a praiseworthy nature through those excellent qualities—such as clarity, radiance, and so forth—which are inclined toward and devoted to that fulfillment. Even the desire of one of noble intent is such.

The teachers are inclined toward the fulfillment of that craving which is the object of desire for all people without exception; they do so by means of their excellent qualities, such as discernment of virtue, generosity,
compassion, and so forth.
Their true nature is praiseworthy.
Furthermore, what is their splendor like?
It was sufficient and complete, spreading out in every direction; it was ample and vast, not merely because of the great number of supplicants observed.
It is contracted.
Furthermore, of what nature is that luster? It is "at the beginning of its rising" (*udayādau*).
At the very beginning of its rising, it is not merely elevated; rather, it is [diminished] by the affliction of the time when the day departs.

Even during the adversity of the time of day’s end, the intention of the magnanimous person remains lofty. It is not merely lofty at the onset of the rise of fortune; rather, even when there is the adversity of the passing of days by the power of destiny, it remains so.
It is indeed elevated; as it has been said:
"The greatness of the great remains uniform in both prosperity and adversity.
Thus spoke Śakreṇdra.
As it is said even in the *Prākṛtagāthāsaptasatī* compiled by the Great King Śālivāhana: "O,
how lofty is this mind of mine!"
In the final moments of his life,
rays of light from the Tathāgata, who was free from all defilements, indeed shot upward.
They do not flash;
"atasya" is the corrected Sanskrit reading.
It remains lofty indeed; it is full of mental vigor even in all conditions,
even at the setting of the sun,
its rays [remain].
They flash upwards indeed;
[this is] in accordance with the verses in the refined language (saṃskṛta).
Since one must speak exactly as the words stand, the fault of breaking the meter (chanda-bhaṅga) is not to be taken into account.
Furthermore, what kind of splendor is it? It is "extreme," such that even for a moment [it is not overcome] by the darkness of gloom.

It is impossible for them to dwell together in one place due to their innate opposition; even the will of the Great-minded One is incapable of dwelling with darkness— the quality of *tamas*— for even a moment,
because it is entirely luminous by nature.
"Āśā, tṛṣṇā, and āyati" also [mean "hope"] according to Amara;
furthermore, "tamas" means Rāhu, darkness, or a quality (guṇa);
[it also means] attachment (abhiṣvaṅga).
And *ruci* is used for longing and for a ray; it is also [used] as a feminine noun. // 24 //

Regarding the word *niḥśeṣā*: may that splendor (*ruci*)—which is like the blazing light, radiance, and beauty of the sun (*bradhna*), or like desire itself—be for you both (*vo yuṣmābhyām*) for the attainment of that desired object. What is it? That which is complete (*niḥśeṣā*), belonging to all...

She whose nature is to be praised and extolled because of her qualities— qualities that are dependent on others, like a flood of the intermediate directions, which is itself inclined toward filling them; she who alone is sufficient for the rising and so forth, and who has reached the limit of pervasiveness.

In this reading, [the word] "atiśayena" means "exceedingly. Not only is she elevated at sunrise and so forth, but even during the *upaplava*— the time or occasion of the day's departure— at twilight as well, she remains elevated by the darkness of gloom (*tamas*).
Even for a single moment, they are utterly and exceedingly unacquainted with dwelling together;
furthermore, their desires are entirely exhausted, as are all hopes and expectations—that is, the mental states characterized by the thought, "May this be mine. In this regard:
She whose essential nature is worthy of praise because of her weighty quality— that which is inclined toward fulfillment and fullness—

is indeed elevated even during the onset of darkness, that period of time characterized by the rising sun and the beginning of her birth, and not merely at its commencement. Even in the midst of that interval, she remains truly exalted despite the darkness.
The meaning is that one should not remain in the same place as an evil person. //24//
Bearing a spear that swiftly quelled the heavy arrogance of the powerful Tāraka, and effortlessly casting even the fire below it into the luster of a shining moon,
it would bring an exceeding delight to the eyes in the midst of darkness.
May Bāla Lakṣmī protect you, like Guha [protects] the boundless power of the Lord of Heaven, and like the sun's heat [protects] the day-maker. 25.
May the fresh sunlight of the Lord of Day bestow upon you boundless prosperity; it is worthy— that is,
capable— of doing so.

The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of requesting (*prārthana*), in the sense of what is fit (*arha*), or in the sense of capability (*śakti*). However, in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), it would be *syāt* according to the rule *āśiṣy ādhair yāt*. This meaning has also been stated previously.
The triad [of attributes] in any case culminates in a benediction (*āśis*). Alternatively, the reading should be *ādheya* [instead of *āśraya*].
Like whom? Like another Guha, namely Skanda; he too was a child always renowned for his perpetual youth. [This is established] by the epithets of both.
He states the similarity with the word "vibhran": that which was quickly and swiftly pacified— the superior, excessive vigor of the *tārakas*, the stars.
By that [splendor], majesty (tejasvitva) is a heavy,
most weighty power or capacity.
Bearing [what]? Of what kind is Skanda?
He by whom the power—the arrogance—of the mighty asura Tāraka has been quelled.
Bearing a heavy and extremely firm *śakti*— a specific type of weapon— he slew Tāraka with that *śakti*.

This is because it is well known in the Purāṇas. Furthermore, of what nature is the heat? It is "acting," that is, effortlessly and with ease producing fire (śikhin) as well as shimmering, radiant moonstones (candrakānti).
Even Skanda, eclipsing and surpassing even the radiance and light of jewels; he who causes them to be outshone.
Even making a peacock— a *śikhin*— his mount for sport; by the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that although a bird is generally unfit to be a mount.
It is revealed that he makes that peacock his vehicle as if in child’s play.
Of what kind is the peacock? "Gleaming" (lasat). It is illuminated by the ends of the very feathers (*kānta*) of the moon-like [spots] which are gleaming.

"One whose beauty is such" means he is thus [described]. This qualification serves as the reason for making the prince a mount; for children, upon seeing various objects, become eager for them for the sake of play.
Furthermore, what kind of splendor did it possess? It was such that it produced an extraordinary delight and pleasure for the eyes— the eyes of all living beings— even in the darkness.

Bestowing light, what kind of person is Skanda? He brings delight to the three eyes of Śiva, the enemy of the Daitya Andhaka. In the phrase "delight in darkness" (*andhakāre rati*), there is the elision of the *ra* sound according to the rule *rori*.
"According to Amara, *śakti* means both capacity and the male organ;
*śikhin* refers to both fire and a peacock."
And "the two moons are equally dark. 25.

"Vibhrāṇam" (bearing): another [comparison], like Guha, like Skanda, or like the young son of the Lord of Day (the Sun) just risen, may he bestow—that is, grant—unto you (*yuṣmākam*) boundless (*apārām*), that is, immeasurable, fortune (*lakṣmīm*). Of what nature [is he]?
Bearing (*vibhrāṇaḥ*) power (*śaktim*), that is, capability. Of what nature [is that power]? That which has been swiftly pacified.

Trampling with ease the feet of powerful stars— that is, surpassing their heavy brilliance— he held even Agni, the fire whose luster is like that of a shimmering moonstone, beneath him with effortless playfulness.
Making the light of the rising sun pale, the white fire-glow becomes manifest; even in the darkness of night,
bringing and generating an extraordinary delight and pleasure for eyes that perceive both [light and dark], Guha too bears his power, wielding his weapons and missiles.
By the majesty of having quelled the powerful Asura Tāraka, he effortlessly surpassed the heavy-peaked peacock; his vehicle, the Sun, shone with a splendor like that of moonstones,
as Mahādeva was being gazed upon by the Andhakas with an exceeding [intensity].
It brings delight;
"bāla" means a youth, and "śikhin" means fire or a peacock—so says the Viśvakośa. // 25 //

At the time of morning's commencement, she unfolds the entire variegated world: her light is entirely white with the rays of moonlight, yet slightly mottled by the darkness that remains; it is tinged with yellow by the pollen of lotuses slightly opened by her yawn, and possesses a crimson luster from the twilight.
May the splendor of the one with piercing rays, bringing incomparable joy to the eyes like a brush, bestow upon you boundless delight. // 26 //
May the brilliance of the sun, with its sharp luster and warm rays, bring you incomparable joy.

May she cause [the world] to attain [its form]. Like what? Like a *tulikā*, a brush for painting a picture. At dawn, at the time of commencement, at the beginning of the morning, she reveals the entire world-picture, which is variegated; or rather, she reveals that very picture as something to be beheld, dispelling the darkness.

Revealing it as if anew by its unfolding, even the brush of a painting produces for the eyes the delight born of beholding a picture. Of what sort is this painted world? It is "moonlight"—that is, a portion of the moonlight.
"Ākṛṣṭi" means drawing forth; that which has a pale luster because of that is "tathā. This is because all moonlight is completely eclipsed by the radiance of the sun.
The meaning is that they possess a pale luster due to the remnants of moonlight.
Furthermore, of what nature [is it]? "In darkness," etc.; it is variegated by the residue of ink, which is indeed the darkness.
Variegated.
Furthermore, of what kind? "Slightly," meaning slightly yawning.
He was tawny (*piṅga*) due to the pollen (*rajas*), the yellowish dust of the lotuses that had blossomed; furthermore, how was he? By the twilight (*sandhyā*).
"Śoṇaṃ" means that whose radiance or brilliance is red; likewise, even a painting on a canvas or similar surface is brought to life by means of a brush and many colors.
"According to Amarasimha: *tūla* [is used] for a multicolored decorative design (*citropakāra*), and *śalākā* for a bed of cotton (*tūlaśayyā*).
A small amount of cotton is called *tūlikā*; the feminine gender is used here in the sense of 'small.
Furthermore, according to Amarasimha: *ālekhyāścarya* is *citra* (a painting). // 26 //

"Jyotsnāṃśā" means: may the brilliance of you who possess sharp splendor, like a stylus or a measuring rod, bring incomparable joy to your eyes. Of what nature is it? At dawn, at the time of commencement.

Unfolding and illuminating the entire world as if it were a painting—like a brushstroke (*tūlikā*) unfolding a painting—what kind of world-painting is it? It is a world-painting that is not entirely white, possessing a luster and shadow due to a portion of moonlight;
for a painting, too, is thus characterized by white luster and dark shadows. Of her...

By the remainder [of the description], its luster is variegated; it is speckled with black from the soot of the artist's charcoal, likewise tawny from the pollen of lotuses produced by the light of a slight yawn, and red from the twilight—its brilliance being thus multicolored. //26//
Is this the path from Mount Sumeru coming here, reddened by the pollen of lotus-gems?
Or is it the Vaijayantī banner of his own chariot, fashioned from mahāraja flowers? Or is it a row of crimson chowries on the heads of the side-horses, shaken by the world? It appears crimson indeed.
May the dawn-light of the Sun, which dispels the darkness and whose crimson hue is as certain as the sight of heaven itself, be for your removal of sin. 27.
May the radiance of Savitṛ, which is being gazed upon by the worlds and thus suspected [of being something else] in this way, shine upon you today. Of what sort is it? It is as follows.
Having reflected in many ways, he states the worldly reasoning: "They are coming. This refers to the path or line of the road coming from the vicinity of Mount Sumeru.
What kind of path is it? It is a path reddened by *padmarāga*— that is, by the pollen (*parāga*) associated with rubies—
which, because the path of Mount Sumeru is overspread with ruby gems,
is crushed by the treading of the feet of those traveling along the way.

The meaning is that it is slightly reddened by fine particles of ruby (*padmarāga*). Or rather, this is the Vaijayantī banner fashioned from *māhārajana*, a cloth dyed with safflower (*kusumbha*), belonging to his own chariot.

Now, alternatively: *māñjiṣṭī* means *mañjiṣṭā*, a particular medicinal herb; [the word refers to something] dyed with that. *Praṣṭha* means those who go before or lead; by the rows (*āvalī*) of them, they were shaken (*vidhuta*).
This row of chowries is the line of their heads; the shaking of heads by the horses occurs during their movement.
Regarding the phrase "the intrinsic nature of the genus": the two words *māhārajana* and *māñjiṣṭī*.

Therefore, when the suffix *taddhita* [denoting color] is established as "red-dyed" (*raktarāga*) and so forth, by the power of proximity with the word *vaijayantī*, the qualified object—the garment—is expressed by the qualifying term *māhārajana*. As it is said: "The flower of the *syāma* tree is neuter; the *karaka* is masculine; *mañjiṣṭhā*, *vikasā*, and *jiṅgī* [are feminine]."
*Sam-aṅgā-kāla-meṣikā*, *puro-gā-agra-sara*, *praviṣṭhā-agrataḥ-sara*, and *puraḥ-sarāḥ* [mean "one who goes before" or "a leader"].

Regarding the particles *āho*, *utāho*, and *kimuta*: according to Amara, they are used in the sense of alternatives (*vikalpa*), as well as in questions (*praśna*), deliberation (*vitarke*), inquiry (*anupṛcchā*), and doubt (*vikalpe*). // 27 //
"Coming," [it is said]. May the radiance of the Sun, which dispels the gloom, be for the destruction of sin. Of what nature is it?

It is perceived by the worlds; thus, in this manner, it is suspected or conjectured. How is it that the path is coming from Sumeru, reddened by the pollens associated with rubies? The "path" (saraṇi) refers to the way.
Is this perhaps the Vaijayantī banner of the chariot, fashioned from saffron-dyed silk? Or is it the driver, clad in crimson madder, who leads the way at the front?
Is it perhaps the row of chowries on their heads shaken by the line of horses? "Nu" is used for deliberation;
"āho vid" indicates an alternative possibility. // 27 //

That which destroys the darkness, yet does not burn intensely, nor reveals its supreme form even when it has brought about its own concealment at night; that which, having withdrawn its brilliance, does not bestow upon the day such radiance as it possesses—[that sun]... [concealment].
May that Sun,
who fulfills your hopes with his form complete and whose youthful rays begin their descent into the expanse of the quarters of the sky, not cease even at dawn. 28.
O Taruṇa; that Sun is young.

May the Light, fulfilling your hope—that is, your desire—not cease; let it not stop, but rather fulfill it at all times. What is that? It is that which effects the destruction of darkness. But not... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
It burns intensely; its exceedingly beautiful, transcendent form does not manifest or reveal itself. Furthermore, it has abandoned the shortness of the night.
Even after taking away the light—that is, the brilliance—of the day, that which does not bestow it exceedingly, does not grant it in excess.
Of what nature is it? "Incomplete" (asakala); in the manner previously described, it is incomplete, not whole, during the morning time.
The meaning is that his image, while appearing as if powerless, is in reality possessed of great majesty.
He says this very thing with the words "of space" (ākāśa), etc.;
[it refers to] the quarters of space.
And that which is the space of the directions;
the ground, the descent there, and the pervasiveness everywhere—therein he is youthful and firm.
*Prakrama* means undertaking (*upakrama*).
He who possesses such exertion is thus [described]; at dawn, he rises subtly, and due to his brilliance, he possesses great prowess. From "mahā... [the word *mahāparākrama* is derived].
The meaning is: "possessing great splendor" (*tejasvin*); "great" (*māhā*) refers to that which is possessed of splendor.
According to Amara, *nyaṅ*, *nīca*, *kharva*, and *hrasva* are synonyms; thus, "being lowly" (*nīcabhāva*) means "concealed" (*nyakta*). 28.

Regarding the word *dhvānta* (darkness): because it is the time of morning, its *paṭimā*—its clarity—is *asakala*, meaning incomplete; this refers to the descent of that [light] into the intermediate space (*avakāśa*) between the sky and the quarters (*diś*). In this regard, its *prakrama* (progression) is *taruṇa*, meaning not yet full-grown.
May that light of the sun, fulfilling your hope, not cease; may it not stop.
Who is he? He who effects the destruction of darkness, bringing about the complete dispelling of gloom.

It does not, to an excessive degree, manifest or reveal its form as heat by means of whiteness and so forth; nor, even having brought the night—that is, the state of being hidden or subordinated—to an end, does it bestow the brilliance of the day in a more abundant measure, because it occurs in the morning. //28//

That which is intense, that which is the cause of Nirvana, that which is vast, that which is exceedingly subtle, that which is perceptible, that which is beyond perception, that which exists here, that which is other, that which is perishable, and that which is eternal;
that which is renowned everywhere in the world and which only a few yogins know.
May that light of the sun, which is of two kinds—external and internal—protect you. 29.

May the two-fold light of Savitṛ protect you, O venerable one. He explains its two-fold nature as follows: "the external" (bāhya) means that which has issued forth from the solar orb; "the internal" (ābhyantara)...

The Brahma-light situated in the space of the heart is described in the Upaniṣads. By way of distinguishing between the two from one another, each is qualified as "intense" (*tīvra*). What is the external like? It is intense and sharp. The internal—

Of what nature is it? It is the cause of nirvāṇa, which is liberation, and is exceedingly gentle. Furthermore, it is vast and extensive. What is the second like? It is extremely subtle; because it transcends the senses, it is described as subtle. Furthermore, one is perceptible, while the second is imperceptible and invisible.

Furthermore, that which exists here in this world is non-eternal and sets; the second, however, is eternal and fixed. Furthermore, that [which exists] outside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), situated as Brahman, is the other.
Furthermore, that which is non-eternal sets; the second, however, is eternal and fixed. Furthermore, that...

It is known as that which is famous to everyone in the world; the second, however, is that which only a few—those very few who are yogins—know. In the word *sarvasya*, the genitive case is used in the sense of "remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī-śeṣe*). In the word *katipaye*, because it optionally functions as a pronoun according to the rule beginning with *prathama-carama-ādi*, the form *katipaye* arises from the substitution of *śī* for *jas*. Thus, the form is external (*bāhyam*).
The elision of the genitive case ending after the word *bahiḥ* is established in the sense of "being outside" (or "external existence"). // 29 //

"Intense": that light of Savitṛ, both external and internal—and for that very reason twofold—may it protect you, may it guard you. What is it? That which is intense, sharp, and the cause of *nirvāṇa*, of liberation. And also that which...

And whatever is vast and whatever is pre-eminently minute and subtle; whatever is perceptible, fit for direct vision, and whatever is imperceptible, invisible; whatever exists here in this world that is supreme, perishable and subject to destruction, and whatever is eternal and constant.
By the principle of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*), [the word] *jagati* [is connected with both preceding and following terms]:

that which is renowned and famous throughout the entire world (an alternative reading is *sarvasya*); and that which some yogins know in the world—yogins themselves being twofold due to the distinction between external and internal; therefore, that [knowledge] is also twofold. //29//
It serves to adorn jewels, having obtained its opportunity through a restricted location.
May that which is the burning of the fire to consume wood and the like through its own dullness,
yet which is the act of adorning the three worlds and the destroyer of sin— being delightful through its rain— swiftly bestow prosperity upon you.
Due to the abundance of the produced effects, a single solar radiance appears as if it were manifold. // 30 //
*Tejaḥ*; *mojaḥ* is then the splendor related to the sun (*arka*), pertaining to Sūrya.
May your splendor protect you. What is that?

It is that which, being produced predominantly as a single entity yet in great multiplicity through its effects, is more preeminent and most distinguished than the splendor of others. He states this very point:
Regarding the phrase "of jewels":
it serves as the ornament for the vital energy (*ojas*) of jewels. Of what nature is that? It is "fixed" (*niyata*);
that is, the place where it is situated is fixed and constant.
Space is that which has obtained its locus by being situated within the head, hands, eyes, arms, and so forth;
having remained in those various places, it is delimited by each of them respectively.
Furthermore,
fire is capable of burning even substantial objects such as grass and wood by means of its vigor.
Furthermore, the moon’s own essence— its dullness, that is, its coldness—
is capable of producing bliss only for those scorched by fire and heat, due to the intensity or excess of that [coldness]. As for its being the ornament of the three worlds, that is merely its limit.
This is the ultimate pinnacle; beyond this, there is no other ornament for the three worlds.
Furthermore, it is the burning away of sin—that very evil which cannot be consumed even by fire.
Furthermore, it is delightful through rain;
it possesses the nature of gladdening all beings by means of the rain produced from its own rays and generated by wealth. Therefore:

The meaning is that it is "the one alone" because, through its distinction from others, it is incapable of being surpassed by anything else and is capable of performing many functions; thus, it is "supremely excellent. In this regard, the reading "ekamevārka-tejaḥ" (the one alone is the solar radiance) is observed in many manuscripts; therein, the word *tejaḥ*—

Because [the word *oja*] is included within a compound, it lacks the capacity for grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with "jewels" (*ratna*) and so forth; therefore, it appears that the reading of our own tradition is simply *ekamevārka ojaḥ*. It has been explained according to that [reading], even though such usage occurs in other poetic works.
Although that reading can also be supported by the force of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), nevertheless,
the elevation of the difficult reading [is established] from the mouth of Mayūrabhaṭṭa, who was graced by the venerable Sun-god.

Regarding the word *saratīti*, we have determined the reading to be *ekamevārkamojaḥ*. In some manuscripts, due to dissatisfaction with this very reading, the variant *ekamarkāsya tejaḥ* has been written;
however, because the word *sat* is necessary, the previously established [reading] is maintained.
It should be disregarded because of its extreme divergence from the reading and because of the resulting looseness of the argument;
for Amara states: "atiśaya means intensity (bhara). // 30 //

Regarding the phrase "of jewels": having produced many more than one single being, that which is to be done—may that singular light, which is the support for the entire world and is connected to the sun and moon, protect you. He speaks of this very preeminence in the verse concerning the limited enumeration of jewels.

Having found an opening in the neck and secured its place, it is capable of serving as an ornament for the circle of light. Fire is capable of burning wood and other such things; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), grass and the like are included.
The light of the moon, through its own inherent dullness—that is, its coldness—is capable of producing joy through its coolness.
What is that? That which is the limit of the ornament of the three worlds is the work of jewels;
that which is seen as the burner of evil and the destroyer of sin is the work of fire; and that which quickly produces joy and happiness through rain is [the work of water].
The function of the moon: the meaning is that it performs as one that does exactly what is performed by jewels and other such things. //30//
With eyes closing, ears dulled, the tongue rendered numb, the function of the nose obstructed, the skin incapable of its own activity, the mind stolen away, and remaining as nothing but mere breath;

May the ancient heat of the sun-born [Agni], falling with its limbs relaxed and removing its own lack of splendor, raise up the world—which has been bitten by the serpent of Time—just as a medicine restores one who has fallen with relaxed limbs and is bereft of fortune. 31.

Born of the Arka plant, produced from the Sun, may your splendor remove our misfortune and ill-fortune! What is it doing? Previously, [it consumed] that which was bitten by the serpent of Time—[the night] in the form of the Destroyer.
Seeing the world bitten by a serpent— a black cobra— they restored it to life, removing the poison of darkness and awakening it.

First, however, there is the incidental fruit of its arising; but what should be said regarding the subsequent, ineffable fruit? What is it like? It is like a great medicine that acts as an antidote. Of what kind is it?

"Jagat"? It means "closing. That whose eyes are closing is described as such. Furthermore, "vijihne" is a specific term for "jihne," meaning sluggish; "śrutikarṇau" refers to ears incapable of perceiving sound.

Whose [tongue] was such; furthermore, whose tongue was incapable of perceiving the essence of flavors—that is how it was; furthermore, whose function of the nose—the power of perceiving odors—was obstructed, meaning it had become distant.
Being thus, moreover, his skin was incapable of the tactile cognition that is its own function; furthermore,
he was one whose mind was overwhelmed by sleep and fainting.
That is so; furthermore, it is stolen away by sleep and fainting,
and is sluggish.

"Whose mind is thus"—that is, whose [mind] is in that state; furthermore, "of whom only breath remains," meaning there is no activity whatsoever of the sense faculties. Having fallen down in such a way that the limbs are completely relaxed and limp.
Even one bitten by a black cobra remains thus [unconscious],
yet such a great medicinal herb restores even one in such a state.
The meaning is that the heat of the sun is equal to that [poison] at first, and subsequently becomes even greater than it.
*Jihma*, however, means crooked or lazy;
*bheṣaja*, *auṣadha*, and *bhaiṣajya* mean medicine, as do *agada* and *jāyu*, according to Amara. // 31 //

"Closing": like an antidote, as a physician for poison revives one bitten by a black serpent (*kālasarpa*), so may the radiance of the Sun-born, which first spreads its brilliance in the east, dispel your misfortune (*aśrī*)— that is, your lack of prosperity— as it raises up the world.
Of what nature was the world? Its eyes were closing due to lassitude; its ears were distorted;
and its tongue was inert, its function being void.
For whom the function of the nose has been obstructed, whose capacity for its own operation— the perception of touch— has been impaired, and whose power of cognition has been stolen away.
He whose mind was composed, who lay fallen upon his bed like a serpent with its limbs relaxed, having only his breath remaining— having been seen and raised up by him,
he indeed rose up.
The sequence for the visualization (dṛṣṭi) is also as follows. 31.

Swiftly dispelling the nocturnal waters without remainder, resembling a falling tear-drop, and gradually removing its lingering crimson glow, the sun has at last cast off the attachment of its evening taint.

May the giver of this collyrium quickly grant you a clear vision of the Eye of the Three Worlds; may the other ancient method of perfected ointment— the spreading of the sun’s rays— destroy that which is adverse to you.
May the eastern radiance—the ancient, forward-moving light—of the sun destroy (vadhyāt) that which is contrary to you, that which is harmful to you.
Of what nature is it? It is "another," meaning of a different kind; this is an elliptical metaphor (luptotprekṣā), suggesting it is like the application of a perfected ointment.
Doing what? "Entirely," meaning forcibly dispelling— that is, removing— the nocturnal water, which is the water consisting of the dew fallen at night.
Of what nature is the water? It resembles a drop of tears, having the appearance of shedding tears. Furthermore, of what nature is the flame? Its movement.

"Stokam" means a little, or something slight. It refers to that by which the luster of Aruṇa, the charioteer, has been somewhat removed—that is, its own radiance has eclipsed the splendor of Aruṇa. Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is one whose nature is giving, bestowing a clear and stainless gaze—the very function of seeing—of the Eye of the Three Worlds, by dispelling the darkness. Furthermore, what is he like?
He has quickly and immediately cast off the attachment to faults; "doṣā" means night, and "anuṣaṅga" refers to its persistence.
The connection is by means of which;

"of the eye" (*nayanasya*)—the singular number is used because it refers to the genus (*jāti*). Even the procedure for the accomplished ointment (*siddhāñjana*) [removes] the flow of tears born from a disorder of the eye.

First, it removes [the obstruction] and drives away a certain degree of redness; it eliminates the persistence of the humors such as wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), and subsequently, having dispelled the disease of cataracts (timira).

"He bestows clear vision" (*svacchāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ prayacchati*): the suffix *tṛn* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), forming the word *dātā*. When this [suffix] is joined with the word *dṛṣṭim*, the prohibition of the genitive case for the object—expressed by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛṇām*—is applied.
"Defects" (doṣa) refers to the humors such as wind (vāta) and others; "at night" (rātrau), according to Amara.
Regarding the form "vadhyāt," this is the form of the root *han* in the optative (vidhi-liṅ) with the substitution of *vadh* for *han*, following the rule that *han* takes the substitute *vadh*. 32.

"Without remainder" means: may the ancient, eastward-moving radiance of the sun destroy, in opposition to you, the enemy and evil; for what kind of being is he? He is one whose method of [attaining] the perfected ointment (*siddhāñjana*) is supreme.

Forcefully dispelling the nocturnal waters in their entirety—that is, the water produced by the night—what kind of water was it? It resembled, that is, was similar to, a few drops of tears; it was such that the redness [of the dawn] had been removed little by little, that is, very gradually.

He by whom [the sun] was cast down before long; he who abandoned the night, which is the attachment—that is, the connection—with the dwelling of the three worlds; or, according to another reading, "he who bestowed a gracious glance upon the eye of the three worlds.

Because of the prohibition against the genitive case in the rule *na lokāvyaya-*, the genitive is not used; thus, the accusative case is established even for the application of the *añjana* collyrium.
It removes the flow of tears and the redness of the eyes; by eliminating the defects of the humors such as bile and phlegm, it bestows a clear vision. 32.
Having first become the source of Jambha’s defeat at the eastern quarter, and then assuming a tawny hue as she boldly blossomed like a fresh lotus,
the radiance of the sun— the ornament of this palace of the three worlds— possessing the greatest splendor, shone forth.
The world; the eastern world.
May that splendor, shining amidst all delusions, bring about the manifestation of your prosperity. 33.
That which belongs to Vaibhākara is indeed yours.
May that radiance, the splendor belonging to the Sun, flourish for your manifestation of power— that is, for the arising of your sovereignty.
Let it be especially so.

Who is she? She who is the ornament—the adornment—of the abode of the three worlds, where the three worlds themselves constitute the abode or house. Of what nature is this ornament? It is an ornament of abundant splendor, possessing great radiance.
What is it like? Having become and remained upon the peak of Jambha-bhettṛ, Indra, it possesses the bright luster of white rays.
She is the ground for the moon's undertaking of humiliation, the locus for its undertaking of disparagement;
furthermore, she bears a tawny state, a brownish-yellow hue. Again, of what nature is she?
"Fresh"—forcibly, by means of fresh lotuses.
That which is yawning is expansion; therein she is bold and mature. Furthermore, of what sort is she?
She is shining and resplendent with *vibhrānti*—that is, with playful confusion or graceful charm (*vilāsa*).
According to Amara, *babhru* refers to the mongoose (*nakula*) and Viṣṇu when used in the masculine, and to "tawny" (*piṅgala*) when used as a term for all three genders.
Here, there is an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) based on the letter *bha*. // 33 //

"Having become," [it means] that radiance belonging to the Sun (Vaibhākarī), which is being made to shine by its own brilliance—may that radiance (*vibhā*) of yours prevail for the manifestation of your prosperity. What is it?
That which has the three worlds themselves as its abode.
Her ornamentation was such that its splendor was exceedingly abundant; having done what? [She stood] in the quarter—the eastern direction—of Indra, the terrifier and destroyer of the Daitya Jambha.
In the "kakubh," that is, in the eastern direction;
having become the "kakubh," the eastern direction, it is the site for the commencement of the eclipse of the moon, whose light is white.

Bearing a tawny hue and a brownish tint—the very ground for being treated with contempt—she boldly and excessively assumed a fresh state; she was confident in manifesting the expansion of that [state] of the Bhoja. 33.
It was sprinkled and moistened at its roots by her who was eager for the new garden of the world.
(The word *saṃsakta* here means "sprinkled.")
By the night, as if by a maiden, with nectar drawn forth from the jar of the moon.
May the light of the sun bring you joy—the first sprout of the tree of day, rising from the basin of the horizon at the peak of its ascent, possessing a luster like that of a young coral shoot. 34.

May the light of the sun bring you joy. Of what nature is it? It is the first sprout—the initial bud—of the day-tree, which is the tree in the form of the day. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "the rising," [the rising of the sun].
The eastern mountain’s head—the Cakravāla range, which is its crown-circle—is itself the basin.
Emerging, that is, appearing from what kind of place? From that which is "closely joined" (saṃsakta) with the night, which is in the form of a woman.
Like the moon, the maker of nectar,
by that very jar when it was turned down— that is, emptied— of its nectar, [the body] was continuously sprinkled throughout the four watches of the night.
From that [tree] whose root was watered to its very end—by what kind of night? By a maiden who is "abhinava"; *abhinava* means fresh or new.
In that world, the garden of the gods, she who was full of curiosity and wonder [asked]: "What is the light of the sun like? [The answer is:
"Like a young shoot"—that is, like the luster of fresh coral (*vidruma*), which is similar to it.
He is one who possesses radiance. Furthermore, it is the nature of a maiden that, out of curiosity, having fashioned a basin for the sake of sport, she [places something] therein.
Having sown a tree seed, one sprinkles it with water from a jar;
then,
due to the inherent nature of the seed, the production of a sprout occurs— this is a statement concerning the general principle.
"Āloka" means vision and illumination;
"udaya" refers to the eastern mountain;
and "cakravāla" refers to the circular horizon.
"Muktā" (pearl) and "vidruma" (coral) are masculine; "pravāla" is both masculine and neuter.
According to Amarasimha, "pravāla" is also used for a sprout and is not feminine. // 34 //
"Entwined" means: may the light of the sun bring you joy. Of what nature is it? It is like a tree of day.

Its "first sprout"—that is, its initial fresh leaf—is dense. Just as another tree's sprout emerges from a basin (*ālavāla*), from what kind of basin? From that which is the basin for the world (*bhuvana*) that is ever-new.
The crest-circle of the eastern mountain, whose luster is equal to coral—that is, to *vidruma*—is like its basin (*ālavāla*).
For when rising, even another tree with coral-like sprouts emerges from a basin. From what kind of basin? From one that is fresh...

The world was like that garden; for the maiden Night, who was full of curiosity for it, the moon—the bearer of nectar—was like a water-pot. Just as a root is thoroughly sprinkled when supplied with the water of nectar by that [pot], so too was the garden sprinkled from that very source. Furthermore, the garden was provided with a basin (*ālavāla*).
The root becomes sprinkled with water brought in a jar by a curious maiden. // 34 //
In some places, it was as if divided by the fresh luster of coral, reddened by the glow of dawn;
in other places, its interior was made formidable by the massed radiance of the jewels of the stars;
and drinking up the heap of darkness that possessed an entirely black splendor within, like the ocean itself—so he gazed.
Though ancient, he is as if unprecedented—a descendant of Durvasa with the brilliance of the sun, for the burning away of your sins.
The eastern radiance,
the light of the sun, exists for the burning away of one's sins.
May he exist for the burning away of your misdeeds;
like what?
It was an unprecedented, novel, and extraordinary Aurva fire, like the submarine fire (Vāḍava-anala). Of what sort?

Though "prior" (pūrva)—meaning delimited by the eastern direction—it is also "unprecedented" (apūrva); by the word "api," a contradiction is suggested, namely that it is both prior and unprecedented. The resolution of this, however, lies in the difference of meaning. What was it doing? [It was consuming] the mass of darkness...
Drinking and drying up; like what? Like the ocean; just as the submarine fire (aurvāgni) [dries up] the ocean.

He drinks in that same manner. Of what sort is the mass of darkness? In certain places it is "united with the fresh radiance of the dawn," meaning it is touched by the light of the sun's rays as they spread over a small area;
with what is it like? It is like the ocean mingled with the luster of corals (*vidruma*).
Furthermore, of what nature is it? In some places, there is a mass of luster belonging to the very stars— which are like jewels— as they move and spread here and there.
The intermediate space was such that it was filled—meaning rendered jagged or uneven—by a mass of luster; its interior was of this nature.
Even the ocean possesses an interior made jagged by the mass of the radiance of jewels resembling stars. Furthermore...
What kind of mass of darkness? "Within" means that its black splendor (kānti) is entirely complete within its interior. What kind of ocean?
Within its midst, the serpent Śeṣa is firmly established.
That in which Kṛṣṇa is Śrī-Nārāyaṇa and Śrī is Lakṣmī, as stated in the Purāṇas.

The meaning is that the splendor of Śeṣa and Kṛṣṇa is certain. In this manner, there is a similarity between the radiance of the sun and the Aurva fire; however, while the Aurva fire is capable of consuming only the ocean, this [fire] has drunk the fire within you and even your sin.
