"Capable of burning"—thus [it is explained]. "Bhinnam" (broken/divided) is a form of the verbal root *bhid*, which has the sense of "joining together" (*saṃsarga*);
its usage as "sambheda" is well-known. In the lexicon, "sambheda" is defined as the confluence of rivers (*sindhu-saṅgama*), and it is used even for mere conjunction in general.
As employed by Govardhanācārya in his *Saptaśatī* (The Seven Hundred Verses), which is composed in refined Sanskrit:
"One whose heart is placed far away, whose secret is hidden, and who is exceedingly hard."
"The embrace of the wicked becomes a separation"—
thus [it is said]; "karāla" means "dantura" (buck-toothed) or "tuṅga" (high/protruding)— so says Amara.

In the case of "niḥśeṣa" referring to the ocean, [the meaning] is determined as "that in which the splendor of Śeṣa-Kṛṣṇa remains. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), according to the rule *prādibhyo dhātujasya*. It is like the expressions "a tree that is an effort" (*prayatno vṛkṣaḥ*) or "a sky without clouds" (*vyabhraṃ nabhaḥ*). [The form] "pluṣṭaye" [is used].
The expression "pluṣṭadāha" (burning heat) is a statement of the abstract state (bhāva) derived from the verbal root. 35.

"Bhinnam" means: he who drinks the mass of darkness like the ocean— that mass of darkness from which all the remaining splendor of Kṛṣṇa has been drawn out within, or where the remaining splendor of Kṛṣṇa has departed because of his dwelling there— just as the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), the unprecedented fire of the ocean-dweller, drinks up the sea.

The light of the sun arises for the nourishment of the world and for the burning away of sin; from where does it come? It is shimmering in some places with a fresh reddish glow, as if with the luster of coral, variegated and beautiful, created by the radiance of the jewels of the ocean. Herein lies the splendor of the stars.
The sense is that it has been accomplished. // 35 //

He who, having shattered [the cycle of existence], is praised by Gandharvas with heart-stealing words interwoven in prose and verse, and by the foremost sages such as Nārada and others who know the Vedas, through the playing of musical instruments;
and he, having been attained, causes the world to immediately attain youth once again as it rises.
May this Sun, whose light illuminates the heavens, dispel all your faults today. 36.
The rising of the day-maker,
the sun, has illuminated the sky; the rising of the sun has shone upon the heavens.
O sirs, may that light of illumination split asunder today your faults and misfortunes.

Let him break it! Who is he? He who, together with Gandharvas—the celestial singers—and instrumental music, [speaks] words intermingled and blended with prose and verse: prose being poetry devoid of meter, and verse being that bound by meter.
By them, he was thus praised— praised in a manner that was heart-pleasing and delightful— with the ancient,
primordial Vedic hymns, by means of the Veda, for the purpose of making it known.
He who was praised by sages such as Nārada, who were capable of defining [the truth], having analyzed,
separated, and discerned [it];
and having again approached and attained him in the morning, the world immediately [attains its goal].

He attains, reaches, youth. The meaning is that, having remained as if aged at the end of the day, through connection with [the dawn], he becomes as if attained to youth at dawn, capable of all activities. Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one by whom the sky, the atmosphere, has been illuminated.
By which it is so; therefore, today, regarding the two terms *vādya* and *vādya*, since these four kinds of musical instruments—
known by the names *vāditra* and *ātodya*— are designated as having the same meaning, [the suffix] *yat* is applied.

It should also be understood as having six divisions, as follows: *ātodya* refers to instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*) and the trumpet (*kāhalā*), by which the musical modes (*rāga*) are manifested; whereas *vādya* is that which manifests the rhythmic beats (*tāla*).
The expression "mṛdaṅga-paṇava-ādi" was employed by the poet himself with that specific intention.
"Prose and verse are the work of a poet," according to Amara.
The form *dyatu* is from the root *doṣ*, meaning "to cut off" (*avakhaṇḍana*). [Thus,] they are *avadyāni*.
Thus, in the sense of the prose passage, [the word *avadyapaṇya*] is established as an irregular form (*nipātita*) by the rule beginning with *avadyapaṇya*. 36.
"By the Gandharvas"—
this light of the sun-maker is a radiance;
even today, [he perceives] faults as they truly are.
May he rend and shatter our sins—what kind of being? One whose radiance shines forth instantly, illuminating the heavens and blazing through the sky.
Who is he? Having reached and attained that light, the world once again attains youth.

He attains [that state] by whom he was praised with words that are heart-pleasing, intermingled and mixed with prose and verse by the Gandharvas; and who is to be known as the primordial physician of the Vedas by those for whom he is the primordial [authority].

The meaning is that he was praised—that is, extolled—by those sages such as Nārada and others, who possessed the lute and other instruments, having distinguished [the qualities] by separating them individually. // 36 //

With the moonstones having ceased their outpouring due to the departure of darkness, with the stars becoming thin as their light was eclipsed by the brilliance of the deer-marked moon, and with the medicinal herbs vanishing as their luster was struck down;
she was for a moment perceived from afar like the crescent of the moon rising on the slope of the eastern mountain, momentarily hidden from view.
May the dawn-light protect you, but not that which appears in its full intensity. 37.
May the morning radiance of the moon protect you.

Of what kind of moon? Of one that has been momentarily hidden by the slope of the mountain of sunrise. Of what kind of radiance? One that is being conjectured—imagined to be nearby—due to the aforementioned reasons.
Furthermore, first of all, they do not manifest at all—that is, not in the slightest degree. He states those very causes with the words:
"by means of sounds."

By means of moonstones that were slightly dried up due to the absence of moonlight; furthermore, because the darkness had fallen away from the sky— this is the ellipsis— and moreover, because of the thinning, that is, the disappearance, of the stars.
Furthermore, it is due to the disappearance of that light which belongs to the moon;
and furthermore, due to the dissolution— the resulting invisibility from subtlety— of the medicinal herbs whose splendor has been impaired and whose brilliance has been cast out.
It is well known that medicinal herbs blaze with their own luster during the night; thus [the word] "avānaiḥ" [is used].
The form [of the word] is derived from the root *ūṣ* (meaning "to burn") with the suffix *niṣṭhā*;
by the rule *oditaśca*,
the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix becomes *ṇ*.
*Śuṣka-vāna* means "dry wood," according to Amara;
and *ārāt* signifies both "distant" and "near."
"Rising" refers to the eastern mountain; this is also [an example]. //37//
"By means of the rays"— referring to the morning radiance of the moon, which has just vanished behind the edge of the eastern horizon; for this very reason, it is not yet fully manifest,
appearing only from afar.
Thus being visualized and inferred by them, may her radiance protect you. He states the very reasons [for this]: "by means of dry inhalations for the purpose of drying."
It is not that [the word] *niṣṭhā* is *udita*; rather,
because darkness is destroyed by the moonstones through the removal of obscurity, the suffix *tal* is applied after a *karmadhāraya* compound.

The meaning is: because of the thinning—that is, the waning—of the stars; because of the disappearance of the light of the moon (eṇāṅka); and because of the dissolution of the medicinal herbs whose splendor was impaired, that is, deprived of their luster. // 37 //

May the light of the sun— the light that appears upon the mountain peak at dawn, which has never before been embraced by the rows of forests whose leaves have regained their youth, which avoids the depths of the hollows and slopes,
and which is equal [to all]— may that light bestow the pacification of worldly existence.
O Lord of Day,
the row of bees on the lotus seems to rise up simultaneously with her, as if she were their companion. 38.

May that splendor of the Lord of Day grant you peace—the peace of non-arising—and may it bring about its cessation. What is that splendor? It is that whose companion, as if a friend, is the row of bees, a line of lotus-pollen, at the same time.

It rises, or rather, it ascends simultaneously; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on the rule of the constant association of two companions. Of what nature is the light? It is upon the peak belonging to the mountain of sunrise (audaya).
On the mountain plateau, she has "not not" (na...
na) reached the row of forests on the peaks—that is, it does not mean she has not reached them;
rather, the meaning is that she has indeed already reached them. This is because of the rule stating that two negatives convey the original affirmative sense.
Of what kind of forests? Those whose leaves and foliage have been reddened—that is, turned red—by the rays of the sun;
and those which possess renewed youth, even though they were once aged.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Its hollows have been removed— that is, abandoned— by *tanimā*, which is thinness.
That [river] by which the interior of caves, as well as hollows and deep places, were occupied; because of its thinness, it [reached] the caverns and so forth.
The meaning is that she did not pervade those two. Furthermore, of what nature was she? She was appearing, yet unequal—that is, incomparable.

The meaning is "incomparable. In the words *ālīḍha* and so forth, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*). Alternatively, by relying on the fact that the root *lih*, preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, has the sense of motion (*gatya*), [the suffix is applied] according to the rule beginning with "roots denoting motion" (*gatyartha*).

The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). [In the compound] *ālīḍhapūrvā*, meaning "one who has previously licked," a compound is formed according to the rule for the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. // 38 //
"On the mountain peak"—may that state of the Lord of Day (the Sun) grant you the pacification of non-existence (the cessation of worldly suffering). What is that state?
It is that whose equal, harmonious, and well-disposed companion is the pollen of the lotus, which is like the splendor of royalty.

It rises as if at the same time [as the sun]. Of what nature is it? Appearing and shining upon the peak (*sānu*) of the mountain of sunrise (*udayācala*), it makes the sky appear like a row of forests whose foliage has attained renewed youth through the splendor of those [peaks] reddened by the rays [of the sun]. The word "day" (*dinam*) refers to the sky.
And *mālīḍhe* means that by which the vicinity of a cave—that is, its low-lying region—has been avoided; it is formed with the suffix *karttarikta*. (38)
That which belongs to the waters of the blossoming lotuses, which leads to beauty and not to heat—
that [beauty] of the waters... that [beauty] of the waters.

Nourishing mere light yet not obstructing the vision of those who behold her, first appearing in the east and subsequently purifying the faces of all directions— may this ancient goddess, the sole abode of praise, dispel your sins as she shines forth. 39.
May this ancient radiance of the Sun—this very light now visible there—drive away, that is, remove far from you, your sins, your evils. Which one? That which...
It does not lead to the splendor, beauty, or prosperity of the waters whose lotuses have blossomed.
First, by manifesting his entire majesty,
he nourishes for the eyes— the mere light, that is, the mere function of seeing.
While being visible,
it does not bestow impact or resistance;
furthermore, [it rises] first from the eastern mountain, the mountain of sunrise itself.
"Having purified" (pāvanī) means subsequently having directed [the breath] toward heaven, that is, toward the sky (ākāśam).
She is the purifier, the sanctifier of the quarters of the sky; furthermore,
she is the one primary abode for the words of praise, the terms of eulogy— this being an epithet whose gender does not change.

The word *śabdaḥ*. In the phrase *divam*, because *anu* is a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *anurlakṣaṇe*, when used in conjunction with it, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is applied according to the rule *karmapravacanīya-yukte*. [The word is] *pāvanī*.

In the word *pāvayitrī*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; then, by the rule *striyāṃ ktin*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added because it ends in a short vowel (*at*).
In the phrase *pūrvādrer diṅmukhānām*, the genitive case is used for the object according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*. [The word is] *inaḥ*.
The sun is the lord of radiance; thus says Amara. // 39 //

May that ancient radiance, belonging to the Lord Sūrya—whose path is a blossoming lotus and who is dark-hued (enī)—drive away and destroy our sins. Of what nature is she? She is the sole abode of the words of praise.

The place: first and foremost, she who generates purity for the eastern mountain itself, and who purifies the sky and the atmosphere; furthermore, she who purifies the faces of the quarters—what is she?
She who brings about the splendor— the beauty— of the waters containing blossoming lotuses;
she nourishes not merely the light for the sake of heat, but rather, being visible, she sustains it.
It causes the obstruction of "dṛśām," meaning the eyes; by this, the dawn-like nature of the light is expressed. (39)
By the elaborations of [this work], which is worthy of being the teacher even for Indra— the Lord of Speech— [the speech] of Indra is surpassed;
it is the speech of Indra, surpassing even that of Indra,
and it is the speech of Indra, surpassing even that of Indra.
Of the four faces of the descendants of Viriñca, whose beautiful Ṛg-verses were thus uttered— of those four faces;
[the first] *cā* belongs to the faces.
May that Fire of fierce rays—whoever’s pure conduct cannot be proclaimed even when his ancient glory is clearly distinguished in the hymns—long bestow increasing splendor upon you. 40.
May the ancient, primordial luster and splendor of that Caṇḍārcis, whose rays are warm,

increase and nourish your fortune and prosperity. If the reading is *ciram*, it should be explained as the accusative plural *vaḥ* (you), meaning "may it for a long time (*ciram*) increase and nourish you."

Of what sort is it? It is that which shines, gleaming. Of what? Of him whose deeds, even through the elaborate expansions of the speech of Vācaspati (Bṛhaspati) during worship or rites of adoration, as well as those of the Vairiñcas—those related to Viriñca (Brahmā)—[are celebrated].
And with the elaborations and playful expressions of his four faces, he analyzed this [reality] intensely and extensively in its true nature.
It could not be spoken; it could not be described, because it is difficult to express due to its boundlessness.
Of what kind is his conduct? It is "to be told" (*vācya*). It is pure by virtue of the departure or removal of that which is to be told—namely, censure.
It is stainless. Of what kind?
[It is] such that Indra, the shatterer of mountains, found in them the appropriate teacherhood—the state of being a teacher—of the words of Vācaspati;
that is, they possess the quality of instructing even Indra, despite his being exceedingly wise.

The meaning is "of those who are fit. Of what kind? Of those whose faces are Brahmā’s (vairiñca), by whom beautiful *ṛc* verses have been uttered; that is to say, of those who know the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of all the deities. The state of being a teacher is *ācāryaka*.
In the case of *yopadhādgurūpottamād vuñ*,
the form is derived by applying *vuñ* and then substituting *uraṇ* for the vowel; in the phrase *ucāritarucirarucām*, the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* applies.

There is preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Because the rule for the suffix at the end of a compound is obligatory, there is the form *ṛkyūḥ*. [The word] *ucyeta* is derived from the potential mood (*liṅ*) by the rule *śakiliṅca*. Regarding the word *vācyam*: according to the lexicon, "the words *garhya* and *adhīna* are to be stated [as having the same meaning]," and since the suffix *tavya* has the sense of censure (*vacanindā*), the word *rāpa* (or *rāpadam*) also [functions in that sense].

The sense of censure is implied by the meaning [of the word]; however, the grammatical derivation of the word is as follows: from the verbal root *vac*, by applying Pāṇini’s rules *ṛhalor ṇyat* and *vaco ’śabdasaṃjñāyām ktiḥ*, it is formed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). In the case of *prācyam*, the meaning is "that which exists in the east" (*prāgbhavam*); here, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *prāggavādyat*.
"Prapañca means error and elaboration," according to Amara. 40.

Regarding the phrase "of words": may that splendor and brilliance (*varcas-tejas*) of Caṇḍārcis—which belongs to the East (*prācya*) and has arisen from the East—long augment and increase you all. Of what [splendor]? Of him whose speech is unswerving (*vācyacyuti*).
The words of those for whom even Indra— the shatterer of mountains— is a fit teacher, [words] whose pure conduct for the benefit of others surpasses that of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods.

If one cannot discern— that is, distinguish individually— the various elaborations (*prapañca*) within the ritual worship (*arcā*) and offerings (*pūjā*), then such [elaborations] are uttered by those belonging to Vairiñca,
that is, those connected with Brahmā; for them, the *ṛc* verses are beautiful.
It is not expressed through the conceptual elaborations of the four faces. // 40 //
Upon the peak of the mountain, it becomes a stream; upon the trees, a mass of coral sprouts; in the ocean, a thick cloud of vermilion dust placed upon the heads of the world-elephants;
and at the boundary of the sky, it arises as the golden radiance of the peaks of the celestial mountains.
May that single spot of beauty on the sun’s face at dawn, possessing the redness of a donkey’s leg, grant you protection. 41.
By its crimson hue;
by this redness of the sun, the hot-rayed one, may that region of beauty— the eastern quarter— grant you splendor.

May he grant protection. Who is he? He who arises here and there at dawn with a crimson hue, that is, through redness. Thus it is said: "From the eastern mountain," and so forth. This refers to the mineral pigment of the eastern mountain, the mountain of sunrise; namely, realgar, red arsenic, ochre, and the like.
It has the color of mineral ores;
furthermore, it is like the fresh sprouts newly emerged upon trees; and furthermore, it is like a mass—a multitude—of corals in the ocean.

Furthermore, there is the dense and thick vermilion powder placed upon the heads of the elephants of the quarters— the world-elephants— for the sake of adornment; and furthermore, [it is seen] at the boundary of the sky, in the region of the atmosphere.

"Suraśikharī" refers to Sumeru; "bhūs" means its ground; "tasya hemnaḥ" means of the gold belonging to that [ground]; "prakāśaḥ" means the luster of that gold. In the phrase "pūrvādreḥ," the word "uparibhāge" (on the upper part) is to be supplied from the context; thus, it means "on the eastern mountain."

Or rather, it should be read as "pāṭhyam. In all cases, the locative case is employed here to avoid the consequence of breaking the sequence [of the meter]. According to Amarasimha, *ogha* means a multitude or the current of water. // 41 //
"Atop the head of Indra"—
this [sun], a single portion of the splendor of the sun at dawn, [is] for you, for yourselves.
May he grant and bestow protection. Who is he? He by whom, through his crimson hue, the mineral pigment is produced upon the summit of the mountain Udayācala;
by whom the sprouts are produced among the trees; and by whom the abundance of coral is produced in the ocean.
The thick vermilion powder recently applied to the limbs of the world-elephants— the heads of Airāvata and the others— becomes manifest.
And at the limit of the sky, the radiance of gold produced from the earth of the divine-peaked Sumeru arises. // 41 //
When the moon, having resorted to the summit of the western mountain, had drunk the poison Kālakūṭa that was the darkness,
[the world was illuminated] by the moon.

May the splendor of the rising sun— clearly beheld by the dawn-pārijāta tree with its reddish young shoots, and appearing like Lakṣmī herself resting within the petals of a blooming lotus while wearing a garment of pale yellow— bring you prosperity. 42.
May the Lakṣmī—the splendor—of the sun, the possessor of intense light, be for your welfare. Like what? Like the Lakṣmī of Viṣṇu.

Lakṣmī? Like Padmālayā (the one whose abode is the lotus). Of what sort is she? "Astādrīti": when the moon has taken refuge on the summit—the highest part—of the mountain named Asta; and likewise, when the poison Kālākūṭa, which is darkness in form, namely the Halāhala poison, has been drunk—that is, when it has vanished.
Likewise,

in the east— in the eastern part— of the morning *pārijāta* tree, which by metaphorical indication has sprouts that are nothing other than the red glow of the dawn, manifestation (the first appearance) was attained.
As she rises, she goes toward her ascent; furthermore, of what nature is she? She whose garment is first slightly red and subsequently, in due order, yellow.

There, the sky is perceived with extreme clarity; it is beheld in its own white, radiant form. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "manifest" (sphuṭā); that is, it rests upon the opening of a lotus that is fully blossomed.
Moreover, another fortune of the Lord Rudra rests upon his head—
the moon that emerged from the ocean of milk; yet, by Rudra, the poison Kālakūṭa, which resembles darkness, was likewise placed there.

Having been drunk up, she again becomes manifest in the *pārijāta* tree; she who has arisen truly, who is reddened on all sides (*ārakta*), and who is most clearly gazed upon by Viṣṇu, the wearer of yellow garments (*pītāmbara*) who is devoted (*anurakta*); she whose refuge is the clearly blossomed cup of a lotus.
Such is it. //42//
"From the mountain of the setting sun": may the splendor (*lakṣmī*) of the sharp-rayed one—like Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari—be for your welfare, for your auspiciousness.
He states her similarity [to that Lakṣmī]:
she whose resort is a clearly blossomed lotus bud; such is Śrī as well.
Likewise, when the Lord Mahādeva had resorted to the crest— the head— of the mountain of sunset (Asta), and while it was thus, as if darkness were the Kālakūṭa poison,
having been swallowed there, at that very dawn, the eastern quarter (aruṇa) possessed the sprout— that is, the fresh leaf— of which was [the rising sun].
When the *pārijāta* tree there in the eastern direction attains manifestation and becomes visible,
and when the rising Lakṣmī has taken her place upon the head of the Lord (Śiva), who bears the moon, and when the *kālakūṭa* poison has been swallowed; [then...]
Previously, at first, when it became manifest upon the *pārijāta* tree—whose sprouts are ruddy and whose leaves are red—it arose. Of what nature was it? Previously...
Then, in that sky— the atmosphere which is reddish and yellow— it is observed as even more distinct and clearer.
By that Viṣṇu, who is red-tinted, devoted, and clad in yellow garments, it was likewise [done]. 42.
Neither the ocean is her birthplace, nor are the Kaustubha gem and other jewels born from her womb her kinsmen;
neither is the lotus in her hand, nor is the chest of the enemy of Naraka her dwelling. The enemy of Naraka—
The supreme form of Śiva, the enemy of Naraka, who is the very embodiment of splendor, establishes the cosmic order throughout the three worlds;
she is the supreme form itself.

May that Śrī— who is indeed distinct from the [worldly] form and who has emerged from the orb of the moon of unmitigated brilliance— bestow blessings upon you throughout the three planes of existence.
May he grant [it];
may he grant it to me,
the one whose splendor is not cool.
May that Śrī, who has emerged from the orb of the hot-rayed sun, grant you prosperity.
Of what nature is she? She consists of radiant energy (*tejas*), yet she is like another, well-known Śrī, in the form of a deity;
however, this [Śrī] is of a different kind. He expresses her dissimilarity through the epithets beginning with "not the ocean" (*nodanvān*). She...
Who is she? She whose birthplace is the ocean;
moreover, from her womb—the very belly of the ocean—were born the Kaustubha gem, the moon, and other such treasures.

She whose kinsmen and brothers are not such [as those of others], in whose hand there is no lotus, and furthermore, for whom the chest of the enemy of Naraka—the illustrious Nārāyaṇa—is not a dwelling place. Of what sort is she? "In the three," it says.
Establishing and maintaining the order of the three worlds, as well as the boundaries of space, time, and so forth— she, however, is not like that;
she has emerged from the peak of the orb of the two suns.
Regarding "Śrī": from the blade of the sword (*maṇḍalāgra*) of this exceedingly radiant hero, Fortune (*lakṣmī*) emerges through his valor. Here, the charm lies in the resonance of a popular proverb.
*Kaukṣeyaka*, *maṇḍalāgra*, *karavāla*, and *kṛpāṇa* are synonyms for a sword, according to Amara. (43)
Thus ends the description of the glorious Sun’s rays in forty-three verses.
"May she who has emerged from the edge of the orb of the sun, whose heat is not cool—that Śrī—grant you blessings;
that is to say, may she bestow prosperity upon you. Of what nature is she? In the three levels of the world, [namely] heaven..."
O mortal, she who establishes order and boundaries within the netherworlds, who is like no other,
whose form is splendor,
and whose nature is radiance— that Lakṣmī.

He states the distinction: What is that [Śrī]? She is the one whose form is splendor (tejas), for whom the ocean is the birthplace; those born from the womb of that ocean—Kaustubha, Pārijāta, Uccaiḥśravas, and so forth—are not her kinsmen, that is, they are not her uterine siblings.
She whose hand holds a lotus, whose form is like the chest of Narayana, the enemy of Naraka, and whose dwelling place is the abode of Indra— may that Lakshmi,
whose birthplace is not the ocean but [this land], and whose kinsmen are the Kaustubha gem and others, grant prosperity; she who holds a lotus in her hand.
Hari’s heart is the place of abiding; this is the description of the rays. 43. Saṃ.
May they protect [us], leaping up with agility from the layer of uncrushed gold and stones;
may they protect [us] uncrushed; may they protect [us] uncrushed.
Those horses of the Sun, who have surpassed the speed of the wind with their lame-like gait, traverse the worlds;

for them, even though they travel without any visible sign of their path, the sacrificial fire arising from the jeweled stone-altar of the sun-gem on Mount Meru reveals the way as it rises with its unrestrained brilliance. 44.
Now, the description of the horse in six verses.
May those solar steeds, the *pataṅgas*, protect the worlds. Of what nature are they?
They are "alaṃ" (sufficiently) swift due to their extreme lightness of movement; they are unimpaired.
Rising up in such a way that there was a mass— a multitude— of golden stones from Mount Meru.
Moving by leaping; the meaning is that due to their swiftness of motion, there is not even the touch of their hooves upon those golden stones. Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Lame" (paṅgu).
On account of the slight contempt shown toward the lame Aruṇa,
and by means of that very prompting; the word "api" (even) is to be supplied here [in the sense of] "by the contempt for the lame."

Who are those by whom the speed of the wind has been conquered? Such [persons] conquer the velocity of the wind even when moving slowly due to a deliberate, contemptuous propulsion; what need is there to mention their superior speed when propelled correctly? Or rather, [it refers to] when it is performed by a limping person against a man who is lame.
The meaning is that they disregarded the wind as being like a cripple. Those by whom the speed of the wind was conquered were such;
who were they? Those who were rising, having become exalted and unrestrained.

"Dīpti" means intense radiance. "Dyumaṇi" refers to sun-stones (*sūryakānta*); these themselves are the stone altars (*śilāvedikā*), which are altars constructed of rock. *Jātavedas* is the fire arising from them.
Vahni (the Fire-god) declares the path to those whom he beholds; he causes them to recognize it. To what kind of people? To those who are "vīta"—that is, those from whom [defilements] have departed.
Where there is the removal—that is, the uprooting—of other signs, such that it occurs in this manner for those moving or going;
[this verb] "vah" (to go) is intransitive in the sense of external motion. This is the meaning: due to the swiftness of the movement, [the dust is removed] by the horses' hooves from the path.

Although the path of the horses is not manifested because the golden rocks have not been pulverized and thus lack hoof-marks, the horse-path is nevertheless inferred by the sign of fire produced from sun-stones through contact with the rays of the sun.
Thus [it is said]: "Another Jātavedas also becomes kindled upon the altar. It is stated that the stone altar is Jātavedas.
[This applies] to the eye and the pain [of the head].
According to Amara, the word *paṭala* is neuter when it denotes a collection; it is not [masculine].
Furthermore, *pataṅga* refers to both a bird and the sun, and *vitardi* is a synonym for *vedikā* (an altar or terrace). // 44 //

"May they protect!"—may those *pātaṅga* steeds, the horses belonging to the Sun, protect the three worlds (*jaganti*). Of what nature are they? They are those by whom the speed of the wind was surpassed through the slight impulsion caused by their contempt for the one-footed Aruṇa.

Out of the lightness of ego, they protect their own feet; leaping up excessively, as it were, like a mass of unbroken gold and stone— that is, a collection of gold and rocks that has not been ground into powder.
Going by leaping over [the mountains], the sense is that even the touch of their feet does not occur upon the golden surfaces due to their speed. Who are they?
Those whose path Meru obstructs as they travel.

The sun-gem, the sun-crystal, possesses an unrestrained radiance; the fire, which is the sacrificial altar made of its stone slab, proclaims—what does it proclaim?—the path. What kind of path? It says: "The path."

The meaning is that where there is the rising of another sign, it is inferred by that very sign. The sense is that through contact with the rays of the sun, the sun-gem (sūryakānta) blazes, and from that, knowledge of its path arises.
Scorched on their backs by the rays [of the sun] falling from behind, which, due to extreme proximity,
cause excessive burning;
(pṛṣṭeśu) on their backs.

With their sighs so broad that they traverse the entire path of the three heavens, drying them up through exhaustion by emitting excessive heat; with excessive heat emitted; with excessive heat emitted.

May the horses of the Sun, who possess intense speed, hasten for the destruction of your enemies—those steeds whose foreheads are bent down by necks as straight as the waters of the celestial Ganges flowing nearby. 45.
May the seven horses of the glorious Sun—the possessor of seven flames and seven steeds—hasten, making haste for your protection and for the destruction of what is undesirable.
Of what sort are they? On their backs...
